Project description:
RasmalAI - AI-Powered Security Intelligence Command Center

RasmalAI is a real-time incident correlation and threat intelligence platform that connects your engineering toolchain - GitHub, Slack, and security advisory feeds - into a single AI-powered command center.

Most teams discover incidents reactively: someone notices Slack is on fire, someone else checks GitHub, a third person googles the CVE. RasmalAI connects those dots automatically.

What it does:

At its core, RasmalAI runs a Deploy Regression Detector - it pulls recent GitHub PRs and issues, live Slack messages from your prod-incidents and security-alerts channels, and active GitHub security advisories, then uses AI to find causal links across all three. Did a deploy precede an incident? Does an active CVE affect a service your team just touched? Are Slack patterns suggesting a systemic failure rather than a one-off? RasmalAI answers those questions in seconds, not after a 3am war room.

Built on:
Coral - SQL interface over live GitHub and Slack data, eliminating manual API wrangling
Groq + LLaMA 3.3 70B - sub-second AI inference for correlation analysis and executive summaries
Streamlit - real-time command center UI with zero-rerun live clock, risk metrics, and structured finding cards

Key capabilities:
- Deploy-to-incident correlation with confidence scoring and blast radius estimation
- Advisory-to-system matching - flags when an active CVE maps to something in your stack
- Executive Intelligence Summary for non-technical stakeholders
- Natural language analysis engine for ad-hoc operational queries
- Risk index, active signal count, and system status updated on every run

The insight behind it:

Existing tools - Datadog, PagerDuty, Splunk - are either too expensive for small teams, require weeks of instrumentation, or only work within a single data source. RasmalAI requires no agents, no instrumentation, and no new infrastructure. If your team uses GitHub and Slack, it works today.

---

Tech Stack

Data Layer
Coral - SQL interface over live GitHub and Slack APIs. Used for all data fetching: security advisories, repository activity, and Slack channel messages. Eliminates direct API integration entirely.

AI / Inference
Groq - Ultra-low latency LLM inference API
LLaMA 3.3 70B - Model used for deploy regression correlation, executive intelligence summaries, and the ad-hoc analysis engine

Backend
Python - Core application language
python-dotenv - Environment and secrets management
subprocess - Coral CLI query execution

Frontend / UI

streamlit.components.v1 - Live ticking clock (pure JS, zero Streamlit reruns)
Custom CSS - Dark command center aesthetic, pulse animations, correlation finding cards

Describe how you have used Coral in your:
How we used Coral in RasmalAI:

Coral is the entire data backbone of RasmalAI. Rather than building separate API integrations for GitHub and Slack, we used Coral's SQL interface to query both sources uniformly - treating live SaaS data like database tables.

We run three classes of queries through Coral:

GitHub Intelligence - querying github.advisories for active CVEs by severity, and github.issues for recent repository activity, PR merges, and deploy-related events on our target repo.

Slack Intelligence - querying slack.messages across three channels (prod-incidents, security-alerts, backend-team) ordered by recency, giving us a live feed of what the team is actively responding to.

Incident Correlation - the core feature. We fire all three queries in parallel through Coral, then feed the combined results into our Deploy Regression Detector. Coral's uniform row format meant we could pass GitHub and Slack data into the same LLM prompt without any source-specific parsing or transformation.

Without Coral, this would have required three separate OAuth integrations, three different pagination models, and three different rate limit strategies. Coral collapsed that into SQL, letting us focus entirely on the intelligence layer rather than the data plumbing.

The current bottleneck - and the feature we're most excited about - is that cross-source correlation still relies on an LLM to stitch results together because Coral doesn't yet support semantic JOINs across sources. That's the next frontier.

Project description:
When production breaks, engineers become human JOIN tables - jumping between Sentry, GitHub, and Slack. 
CortexSRE uses Coral SQL to unify those signals in one query, then heals the codebase, opens a real GitHub PR, and notifies Slack - in one autopilot loop.
Describe how you have used Coral in your:
Coral is the relational nervous system of the Cortex-SRE. It transforms fragmented observability data into a single SQL-queryable layer, enabling the agent to reason across Sentry, GitHub, and Slack without manual context-switching.

1. Unified Sensing Layer
Coral ingests Sentry issues, GitHub commits, and Slack history and exposes them as relational tables. A single Coral SQL JOIN correlates an active error with the most recent commit touching the same file and any Slack discussion mentioning it — replacing three separate UI hunts with one query.

2. The Agent's Four-Step Loop
Sense: Coral SQL detects active incidents and returns joined context (stack trace, commit author, chat history).
Plan: The agent inspects the Coral output, test failures, and repo state to form a repair strategy.
Heal: The healer runs pytest, sends the traceback to an LLM (or uses a deterministic fallback for demos), applies the patch, and reruns tests.
Act: On success, the system pushes a branch, opens a real GitHub PR, posts a Slack summary, and logs the run to Coral's cortex_system.runs catalog.

3. File-Backed, Zero-DB Architecture
Coral specs (mock_sources.yaml, live_obs.yaml, cortex_system.yaml) define schemas. In production, REST adapters sync live APIs into local JSONL cache files; Coral reads these directly. No database infrastructure required.

4. Meta-Monitoring
Because every agent run is logged to cortex_system.runs, you can audit the bot's own MTTR and success rate using the same Coral SQL interface the agent uses to sense incidents.

Project description:
ContriMatch is an omnichannel personal agent that automatically connects open-source contributions with career opportunities. It is built entirely on top of Coral — the declarative multi-source SQL engine — and powered by Gemini 3.5 Flash for autonomous natural-language intelligence.

What It Does
ContriMatch solves a real problem every open-source contributor faces: finding the right issues to work on, matching those contributions to real job opportunities, and staying on top of the fast-moving OSS landscape — all from one place. Instead of juggling GitHub, job boards, tech news aggregators, and messaging apps separately, ContriMatch unifies them into a single reactive dashboard with a Telegram bot that works from your phone.

How Coral Powers Everything
Coral is the backbone. Every single data feed in ContriMatch — GitHub Issues, GitHub Pull Requests, Remotive Jobs, Adzuna Jobs, HackerNews stories, DEV.to articles, and Telegram updates — is queried through Coral SQL. There is no custom REST client code, no manual API integration, and no ORM. The application treats every external service as a SQL table. This means I can write queries like:

sql

SELECT g.title AS issue, r.title AS job, r.company_name
FROM github.issues g
JOIN remotive.jobs r ON r.tags LIKE '%react%'
WHERE g.owner = 'facebook' AND g.repo = 'react' AND g.state = 'open'
That single query performs a live cross-source JOIN between GitHub and Remotive — two completely unrelated APIs — and returns combined results in one response. This is something no REST wrapper can do.

The Contribution Moat (22 PRs)
I didn't just use Coral — I built the sources that my project runs on. I authored and submitted 22 pull requests to the Coral repository, of which 18 have been merged and released. These include the community source specs for:

Remotive (PR #685) — remote job metadata queries and tags
HackerNews (PR #803) — Algolia search, story scoring, comments
DEV.to (PR #811) — article querying, reactions, author indices
Adzuna (PR #815) — worldwide job aggregation via table functions

Excludes assigned issues (assignee__login IS NULL)
Filters high-noise issues (comments < 3)
Excludes issues where someone already has an open PR (nested subquery: i.title NOT IN (SELECT p.title FROM github.pulls …))
Cross-references PR titles and bodies against issue numbers to detect collision even when titles don't match exactly
Calculates a quality score (0–100) based on comment count and age to surface easy-to-claim tickets first

The system detects resume analysis intent, routes the text to Gemini, compares it against your live pull requests, and generates specific suggestions like "Your Adzuna source spec (PR #815) is not mentioned in your resume — add this bullet: 'Designed and implemented a declarative job aggregation source specification for the Adzuna API, enabling SQL-queryable worldwide job search across the Coral engine.'"

HackerNews: Searches topics via the Algolia-powered hn.search table. Sort locally by Top Points or Most Recent.
DEV.to: Searches by tag via the devto.articles table. Sort locally by Most Reactions or Most Comments.
Both panels store their data in-memory after the initial fetch and sort purely on the frontend for instant UI updates without re-querying the API.
6. Autonomous Self-Healing NL→SQL Agent The /api/ask endpoint converts any natural-language question into a Coral SQL query using Gemini. If the generated SQL fails at the Coral CLI level (syntax error, schema mismatch), the raw error log is fed back into Gemini with the original question. The agent autonomously regenerates corrected SQL and re-executes — delivering zero-crash reliability. This is the core AI intelligence layer of the project.

7. Bidirectional Telegram Bot A background daemon thread inside FastAPI polls the native telegram.updates Coral source for new messages. When a user texts the bot (e.g., "Find Python developer jobs"), the message is routed through the NL→SQL agent, results are formatted as clickable HTML links, and sent back to the user's phone. Send-to-Telegram buttons on every panel (issues, jobs, articles) to forward items to your phone with one click
Password recovery: If you forget your settings password, the bot sends a temporary reset code to your Telegram
8. Secure Settings Manager API keys (Gemini, GitHub, Telegram) are managed through a password-protected settings panel. Passwords are SHA-256 hashed with random salts. Keys are stored in a .env file and reloaded at runtime. Key updates trigger a Telegram security notification.

9. Glassmorphic Dark/Light Theme Premium UI with HSL-tailored color variables, frosted glass panels, neon accent borders, smooth micro-animations, and session-persisted theme toggle.

Describe how you have used Coral in your:
DevLens uses Coral as its data layer. Coral sits between the FastAPI backend and the five engineering data sources - GitHub, Sentry, Datadog, Linear, and OSV , and exposes all of them through a single SQL interface.

When a user asks a question, the backend builds a SQL query and submits it to the Coral runtime via "coral sql --output json". Coral handles authentication, pagination, and schema normalization for each source independently, so the backend never writes a single API client.

The OSV source runs without authentication and returns real CVE data through Coral whenever the binary is installed. This means every query in the system goes through the Coral execution path regardless of whether live credentials are present.

Coral is also wired into the MCP server config via coral mcp-stdio, which means Claude Desktop can query the same source schemas directly -the same tables the DevLens UI queries are browsable as a natural language tool in Claude.

Describe how you have used Coral in your:

YAML source definitions — for YouTube, Gmail, Codeforces, and Google 
Calendar — each mapping SQL tables directly to REST API endpoints.

runs SQL queries, and returns parsed JSON rows. OAuth tokens are

  (no token needed — public API mapped via Coral)

- Calendar: SELECT summary, start_date_time FROM google_calendar.events

API JSON (e.g. snippet.resourceId.videoId) into flat SQL columns — 
eliminating all manual JSON parsing.

and the backend falls back to direct API calls — so the app always works.
How was your hackathon experience?:
The WeMakeDevs Pirates of the Coral-bean Hackathon came up and the theme was Coral — a tool that lets you query REST APIs using plain SQL. I had never heard of it before. But the idea of treating APIs like database tables genuinely intrigued me, so I signed up solo and started reading the docs.

No single place tells me "hey, you haven't pushed code in 3 days and your LeetCode streak is about to break." I wanted that. So I decided to build it — DevMirror.

The early days were messy. I had to figure out Coral's DSL v3 YAML format from scratch while simultaneously building a FastAPI backend, a React frontend, and wiring up Google OAuth. I wrote 4 custom YAML source definitions — for YouTube, Gmail, Codeforces, and Google Calendar — each mapping SQL tables directly to live API endpoints. The YouTube one was the trickiest because the API returns deeply nested JSON, and I had to use Coral's expr + path system to flatten it into clean SQL columns.

The AI integration broke more times than I'd like to admit. Cohere would rate-limit at the worst moments, so I added Gemini 2.5 Flash as a fallback. The Calendar page had a bug where Coral's internal cache was returning stale events — newly created events weren't showing up. I ended up bypassing Coral for Calendar and fetching live directly from the Google API. Not elegant, but it worked.

Building solo meant every decision was mine — and so was every bug. There were nights where the AI coach was hallucinating calendar event formats, or the Gmail Radar was returning empty results because the OAuth token had silently expired. I learned more about token refresh flows and Fernet encryption in one week than I had in months.

What surprised me most was deciding to contribute the YAML files back to the Coral open source repo. I submitted a PR — and actually got proper code review from the maintainers. They caught that I had written single_events = 'true' instead of single_events = true in the examples. Small thing, but it matters. I fixed it and pushed. My first real open source contribution to someone else's codebase came out of this hackathon.

By the end, DevMirror had a working dashboard, Gmail Radar, YouTube Analyser, an AI coach that creates real calendar events from plain English, and several other features. I shipped it live on Vercel at coraldevmirror.vercel.app.

Project description:
Every team shipping LLM apps pulls in langchain, transformers, pillow, requests — the same Python ecosystem powering your AI stack is also your biggest CVE surface. When a vulnerability drops, your container registry rejects the image, CI goes red, and someone burns 30–60 minutes becoming a human JOIN across OSV, GitHub, Sentry, Jira and Grafana just to answer one question:

"Is this CVE actually being exploited in our running app — and is anyone already fixing it?"

CoralSentinel answers that in ONE cross-source Coral SQL query, then runs a DETECT → RECOMMEND → ACT agent loop on top — with a human in the loop for anything that writes.

⚠️ This is a proof-of-concept built for a one-week hackathon (Pirates of the Coral-bean, WeMakeDevs × Coral). It's not a finished product — it's a demonstration of how far one developer can get on a hard, cross-stack problem when the integration layer is just SQL. The thing doing the heavy lifting is Coral.

🪸 What Coral does here 
• 5 vendor APIs (OSV + GitHub + Jira + Sentry + Grafana) become 5 tables you can JOIN 
• Coral handles auth, pagination and rate limits below deck - I just write SQL • Correlation on time windows + LIKE, not brittle exact keys 
• A custom OSV source spec (Coral DSL v3) turns OSV's search API into a reusable Coral table function

🤖 The agent loop (human-in-the-loop) Recommends a typed action list — open Jira tickets, draft a GitHub PR to bump pillow 9.0 → 10.3, annotate Grafana, generate a posture report. Coral stays strictly read-only; nothing executes until you click Approve. ~30 minutes of correlation → ~30 seconds.

✨ Also in the build 
• Bring-your-own LLM — runs on Cursor, EURI, Grok, or Anthropic 
• Org-scoped login (SQLite + PBKDF2 + http Only sessions, stdlib only) 
• Natural-language → Coral SQL that SHOWS the SQL it ran — zero black box 
• Cached reads + single-container Docker deploy

🧰 Stack: 
Coral SQL 
custom OSV source
FastAPI
React
Cursor / EURI / Grok / Claude
Python 3.10+
Describe how you have used Coral in your: Coral is the entire data layer of CoralSentinel — it's the only thing our code uses to read from any external tool. We never call the GitHub, Sentry, Jira, Grafana, or OSV APIs directly. Instead, Coral turns all five into SQL tables, and our app's job is simply to generate SQL, hand it to Coral, and format the results.
How was your hackathon experience?:
It was a grind, but the good kind.

My first version was too ambitious and I scrapped it. The second time, my cross-source queries kept returning empty — turned out I was matching CVE IDs and timestamps exactly, when real data is messy. Switching to loose LIKE matches and time windows was the moment things finally clicked. Getting Coral running on Windows through WSL also cost me an evening I won't get back.

But somewhere around the third rewrite, I watched five separate tools — OSV, GitHub, Jira, Sentry, Grafana — turn into five tables I could JOIN in one query, and it genuinely felt like cheating. That's the whole reason one person could build this in a week.

I'm shipping it as an honest 80% proof-of-concept, not a polished product. It broke, I fixed it, I rewrote the plan more than once — and I learned more in this week than in a month of normal work.

I didn't deploy it as It is still a work in progress, but I have tried to cover all the features in the Demo Video under 3 minutes.

SELECT i.number, i.title, h.title AS hn_post, s.title AS so_question
FROM gh.issues i
LEFT JOIN hackernews.stories h ON LOWER(h.title) LIKE '%' || LOWER(i.title) || '%'
LEFT JOIN stackoverflow.questions s ON LOWER(s.title) LIKE '%' || LOWER(i.title) || '%'
WHERE i.state = 'open' ORDER BY i.updated_at DESC LIMIT 100

KEVGuard — AI-Powered Dependency Security Scanner

KEVGuard scans any public GitHub repository for vulnerable dependencies and tells you which ones are actively being exploited — in under 10 seconds.

Paste a GitHub URL. Get a security score, a full vulnerability breakdown, and an AI-generated fix plan.

What's under the hood:

NVD fallback for filling in missing CVSS severity scores
EPSS scores from first.org — the probability each CVE gets exploited in the wild within 30 days
Gemini for plain-English AI summaries and prioritized fix recommendations
Supports npm, PyPI, Go, Rust (Cargo), and Maven
Features shown:

Security score with breakdown explanation

Describe how you have used Coral in your:
Coral is the single source of truth for all security intelligence in KEVGuard. Every piece of data the scanner needs — repository files, vulnerability records, and active exploitation status — comes through the Coral bridge via SQL, not through separate REST API integrations.

The core query

The heart of the scanner is a single cross-join SQL query that runs for each dependency:

SELECT v.id, v.summary, v.severity, v.affected, v.references, v.aliases,
       k.cve_id AS kev_cve_id, k.vulnerability_name, k.date_added, k.required_action
FROM osv.query_by_version v
LEFT JOIN cisa_kev.vulnerabilities k
  ON v.aliases LIKE '%' || k.cve_id || '%'
WHERE v.package_name = 'lodash'
  AND v.ecosystem    = 'npm'
  AND v.version      = '4.17.20'
LIMIT 50
This single query joins two completely different data sources — OSV (Open Source Vulnerabilities) and CISA KEV (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities) — in one round trip. Without Coral, this would require two separate API calls, manual CVE ID matching in application code, and stitching the results together. Coral makes it a join.

The join condition v.aliases LIKE '%' || k.cve_id || '%' works because OSV stores CVE IDs in a JSON aliases array. Coral allows string pattern matching across that serialized JSON to match against KEV's cve_id column — a cross-schema join that would be impossible with direct API calls.

Three Coral data sources

github.contents — fetches manifest files directly from any public repository. KEVGuard uses this to pull package.json, requirements.txt, go.mod, Cargo.lock, pom.xml, and other lockfiles without needing a GitHub token or handling pagination.

osv.query_by_version — queries the OSV vulnerability database by package name, ecosystem, and version. Returns the full vulnerability record including CVSS severity vectors, affected version ranges, fix versions, and reference URLs — all as structured columns.

cisa_kev.vulnerabilities — the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. Joined directly against OSV results to flag which vulnerabilities are actively being weaponized in the wild. This is what drives the KEV badge and the score penalty in KEVGuard.

What this enables

Before Coral, building this would mean: GitHub REST API for files, OSV HTTP API for vulns, CISA JSON feed download for KEV, then writing application code to correlate CVE IDs across all three. Three separate integrations, three failure modes, three rate limit budgets.

With Coral, it's one SQL query. The cross-join handles the correlation. The Coral bridge handles the data fetching. The application just processes rows.

The SQL Log tab in KEVGuard's sidebar makes this visible — every query the agent runs is logged with its label, full SQL, row count, and duration. You can watch exactly what Coral is doing for each package scanned.

Project description:
Coral Catalog is a semantic query-planning cache for Coral agents. It automatically discovers relationships across Coral sources — tables, schemas, join paths, investigation recipes — and compresses them into a compact intelligence layer that gets injected into the agent's context at query time.
Instead of burning tokens on schema discovery before every investigation, agents get a pre-built map of exactly where to look and how to join across sources. The result is a 67% reduction in total token usage and an 80% reduction in tool calls on the same investigation tasks — verified live via a built-in A/B evaluation harness that runs both paths simultaneously and compares metrics directly from model response metadata.
The core insight is the distinction between caching answers (what Redis does) and caching understanding (what Coral Catalog does). Every query is different, so caching results doesn't help. But the schema relationships, join paths, and investigation patterns are stable — and precomputing those is what makes agents dramatically more efficient.
Describe how you have used Coral in your:
Coral is the execution layer throughout the project. The catalog generation pipeline uses Coral's coral.tables, coral.columns, and coral.filters metadata tables to inspect connected sources, extract schemas, and detect likely join relationships automatically — no manual configuration required.
At query time, the A/B evaluation harness runs two isolated Coral agents against the same question on the same data source. The cold agent uses only Coral's native source discovery. The catalog agent receives Coral plus the optimized catalog context and is constrained from running redundant schema discovery calls. All data queries in both paths execute as Coral SQL, and the token and tool call metrics are captured directly from the model's response metadata to ensure the comparison is unbiased.
The demo dataset is a synthetic incident response scenario — GitHub PRs, deployments, incidents, Sentry events, Slack messages, and support tickets — configured as a local Coral JSONL source, making the entire project self-contained and reproducible.

Coral is the read-only SQL substrate the entire app runs on. We registered two Coral sources — Stripe (customers, payment intents, charges, refunds, disputes, live balance) and Slack (channels, users, plus messages and thread_replies exposed as table-valued functions). The agent reaches them through Coral's MCP server, configured in .mcp.json and called via mcp__coral__sql. Independent reads run in parallel inside one MCP session.

The product idea is cross-source storytelling, and that's exactly what Coral makes ergonomic. The headline insight — a #finance question about a missing $10 billion transaction — is literally a SQL JOIN between slack.messages(channel => '...') and stripe.payment_intents matched on the payment-intent ID appearing inside the message body:

  ▎
  ▎ SELECT pi.id, pi.amount, pi.status, msgs.ts, msgs.text
  ▎ FROM stripe.payment_intents pi
  ▎ JOIN slack.messages(channel => 'C0...') msgs
  ▎  ON msgs.text LIKE '%' || pi.id || '%';
  ▎

Coral handles all three of the hackathon's required concerns — auth (OAuth for Slack, restricted/test key for Stripe), pagination (Slack's cursored conversation history, Stripe's has_more lists), and rate limits (Slack's tiered buckets, Stripe's burst handling) — so the agent never touches an SDK or writes a single retry loop. the agent treats it as just another relation).

One Coral install replaced two SDKs, two auth flows, two pagination loops, and an ETL job — and gave us a single SQL surface the agent can JOIN across.

ContriMatch is an omnichannel personal agent that automatically connects open-source contributions with career opportunities. It is built entirely on top of Coral — the declarative multi-source SQL engine — and powered by Gemini 3.5 Flash for autonomous natural-language intelligence.

What It Does
ContriMatch solves a real problem every open-source contributor faces: finding the right issues to work on, matching those contributions to real job opportunities, and staying on top of the fast-moving OSS landscape — all from one place. Instead of juggling GitHub, job boards, tech news aggregators, and messaging apps separately, ContriMatch unifies them into a single reactive dashboard with a Telegram bot that works from your phone.

Coral is the backbone. Every single data feed in ContriMatch — GitHub Issues, GitHub Pull Requests, Remotive Jobs, Adzuna Jobs, HackerNews stories, DEV.to articles, and Telegram updates — is queried through Coral SQL. There is no custom REST client code, no manual API integration, and no ORM. The application treats every external service as a SQL table. This means I can write queries like:

sql

SELECT g.title AS issue, r.title AS job, r.company_name
FROM github.issues g
JOIN remotive.jobs r ON r.tags LIKE '%react%'
WHERE g.owner = 'facebook' AND g.repo = 'react' AND g.state = 'open'
That single query performs a live cross-source JOIN between GitHub and Remotive — two completely unrelated APIs — and returns combined results in one response. This is something no REST wrapper can do.

This means ContriMatch's agent doesn't just call Coral — it runs on top of source integrations I personally contributed to the engine. The project and the platform are inseparable.

1. Multi-Repository OSS Issue Tracker Add multiple GitHub repositories (e.g., facebook/react, supabase/supabase) on the fly. Each repository renders its open, unassigned issues in a collapsible, self-contained panel. The engine applies smart deflationary filters:

Excludes assigned issues (assignee__login IS NULL)
Filters high-noise issues (comments < 3)
Excludes issues where someone already has an open PR (nested subquery: i.title NOT IN (SELECT p.title FROM github.pulls …))
Cross-references PR titles and bodies against issue numbers to detect collision even when titles don't match exactly
Calculates a quality score (0–100) based on comment count and age to surface easy-to-claim tickets first

Adzuna: Supports keyword, location, and job type inputs that are concatenated into a clean query. All fields are optional — search with just a keyword, just a location, or both.

HackerNews: Searches topics via the Algolia-powered hn.search table. Sort locally by Top Points or Most Recent.
DEV.to: Searches by tag via the devto.articles table. Sort locally by Most Reactions or Most Comments.
Both panels store their data in-memory after the initial fetch and sort purely on the frontend for instant UI updates without re-querying the API.

If the generated SQL fails at the Coral CLI level (syntax error, schema mismatch), the raw error log is fed back into Gemini with the original question. The agent autonomously regenerates corrected SQL and re-executes — delivering zero-crash reliability. This is the core AI intelligence layer of the project.

The SQL query is also displayed transparently in the CIgnal UI at all times. There is no black box. Any developer reading the query understands exactly what data was fetched, from where, and how it was correlated. Project description:
CrewSight is an OSS Maintainer's Command Center — a personal agent that 
monitors GitHub, Hacker News, Reddit, and Stack Overflow for you and surfaces 
what matters, powered entirely by Coral SQL.

Instead of manually checking 4 platforms, maintainers get one unified 
dashboard with AI-powered triage. The AI agent queries Coral directly via 
MCP (coral mcp-stdio), runs cross-source SQL JOINs across live APIs, and 
writes a prioritized briefing — telling you exactly which issues have 
community buzz and what to act on first.

Coral Features Used:
• SQL interface — all data via coral sql
• Cross-source JOINs — gh.issues × hackernews.stories × stackoverflow.questions
• Schema introspection — coral.tables, coral.columns, coral.table_functions
• Caching — TTL cache on top of Coral's query cache
• MCP integration — LLM queries Coral via coral mcp-stdio

Special Bounty Contributions (new source specs):
• Apache Iggy — message streaming server (streams, topics, consumer groups, stats)
• Baseten — ML model deployment platform (models, deployments, secrets)

Tech Stack: FastAPI, Coral CLI, Next.js, NVIDIA NIM (Llama 3.3 via MCP)
Describe how you have used Coral in your:
CrewSight uses Coral as its entire data layer — every piece of data on the 
dashboard flows through Coral SQL.

1. SQL Interface
All 4 data sources (GitHub, Hacker News, Reddit, Stack Overflow) are queried 
via coral sql --format json. The backend runs Coral as a subprocess and parses 
the JSON output into API responses.

2. Cross-source JOINs
The main dashboard query is a single SQL JOIN across 3 live APIs:

SELECT i.number, i.title, h.title AS hn_post, s.title AS so_question
FROM gh.issues i
LEFT JOIN hackernews.stories h ON LOWER(h.title) LIKE '%' || LOWER(i.title) || '%'
LEFT JOIN stackoverflow.questions s ON LOWER(s.title) LIKE '%' || LOWER(i.title) || '%'
WHERE i.state = 'open' ORDER BY i.updated_at DESC LIMIT 100

One query, three live APIs, returning 100 enriched issues with cross-platform 
buzz scores.

3. Schema Introspection
The /api/schema endpoint queries coral.tables, coral.columns, and 
coral.table_functions to discover all registered sources at runtime.

4. Caching
A Python TTL cache layers on top of Coral's own query cache. POST /api/refresh 
clears both layers to force fresh data.

5. MCP Integration
The AI triage uses coral mcp-stdio as an MCP server. The LLM receives 
Coral's sql and list_catalog tools and queries the data sources itself — 
deciding which SQL to run, executing it via MCP, and writing the briefing 
from the live results. The actual SQL queries Claude ran are shown in the UI.

Reddit's nested JSON structure (data.children[*].data) couldn't be reached 
by Coral's DSL, so a FastAPI proxy endpoint flattens it — Coral queries 
localhost:8000/proxy/reddit and gets a clean flat table back.
How was your hackathon experience?:
Building CrewSight was genuinely fun and frustrating in equal measure.

The hardest part was Reddit. Coral's DSL couldn't reach Reddit's nested 
JSON structure no matter what I tried — rows_path, __ notation, nothing 
worked. I spent way too long on it before realizing the cleanest fix was 
building a proxy endpoint that flattens the response first. That kind of 
"understand the tool's limits and work around them creatively" moment was 
the best part of the hackathon.

MCP was the highlight. Seeing the LLM actually call Coral's sql tool, 
generate its own queries against live data, and write a triage briefing 
from the results — that was the moment the project felt real.

I also submitted 2 community source specs (Apache Iggy and Baseten) — 
they're currently under review. Writing them taught me a lot about how 
Coral models different API patterns, especially nested field access and 
timestamp handling.

Overall — Coral is a genuinely interesting tool and this hackathon was 
a great excuse to push it to its limits.

Project description:
Dependency Risk Auditor — paste any GitHub repo URL and every npm dependency is scored 🟢 healthy / 🟡 watch / 🔴 danger in one click.

Every developer has side projects with quietly rotting dependencies. The 2024 xz-utils backdoor was caught by accident. Tools like Snyk and Dependabot only fire after a CVE is published — nothing watches the three signals that together predict a supply-chain attack before it happens: active CVEs · an abandoned maintainer · collapsing downloads.

This tool watches all three. It reads a repo's package.json and, for each dependency, runs a single Coral SQL query that JOINs three genuinely separate live systems — Google's OSV vulnerability feed, the npm registry, and npm's download API — then a pure, unit-tested scoring function turns the joined row into a verdict. That cross-source JOIN is the whole reason it needs Coral: no single API — and no LLM — can answer "which of my dependencies are vulnerable and abandoned and losing users" in one shot.
Describe how you have used Coral in your:
Coral is the entire data engine of this project — there is no database and no backend ETL; Coral is the data layer.

I wrote three custom Coral source specs (all public, no-auth APIs, validated with coral source test):
• sources/osv.yaml — Google's OSV vulnerability database (POST /v1/query)
• sources/npm.yaml — the npm registry for package metadata, latest version, repo URL, publish dates
• sources/npm_downloads.yaml — npm's download-counts API (last-week / last-month trend)

The core of the app is one Coral SQL query (sql/audit-query.sql) that JOINs all three sources in a single statement — across three different hosts — and returns one row per dependency with CVE count, worst severity, download trend and staleness. It runs on Coral's DataFusion SQL engine using array_agg(named_struct(...)) to fold each package's CVE list into the row and date_part for the staleness math.

Authoring the specs taught me the real Coral details: nested fields need explicit expr: { kind: path } (the __ flatten convention isn't automatic), array indices are string keys ([affected, "0", package, name]), and a declared filter must also be a column to be WHERE-queryable. The app shells out to coral sql … --format json; a transparent HTTP fallback against the same endpoints keeps the demo alive on a machine without the CLI, and the UI labels which path is live so the data is always identical.

The cross-source JOIN is the moment the whole project clicks — three live systems, one result set, zero glue code. That genuinely cannot exist without Coral.
How was your hackathon experience?: Honestly, really fun. I came in not knowing Coral at all, and the moment it clicked was seeing one SQL query JOIN three completely separate APIs — that genuinely changed how I think about pulling data together. The tricky part wasn't the code, it was learning the source-spec quirks (nested paths, string array indices, DataFusion vs SQLite), but each fix felt like a small win. Tight timeline, lots of debugging, but I shipped something I'd actually use. Came out knowing a tool I'll reach for again.

Project description:

Before any deployment, an engineer runs one command "harbourmaster check". Within seconds, Harbourmaster checks six different systems simultaneously — whether CI passed, if the error rate is elevated, if infrastructure metrics are healthy, if there is an active production incident, if any third-party dependencies are degraded, and if the release scope is fully complete. It then produces a clear GO or HOLD verdict with a plain-English explanation of the reasoning, posts an automatic notification to the team's Slack #deployments channel, and logs the decision for future reference.

The problem Harbourmaster solves is one every engineering team experiences but rarely talks about. Answering "is it safe to deploy?" correctly requires checking GitHub, Sentry, Datadog, PagerDuty, StatusGator, and Linear — six separate tools, six separate context switches, 10-15 minutes of manual effort. Under time pressure, engineers skip checks. Skipped checks mean teams deploy into active incidents, ship when error rates are already elevated, or release incomplete milestones. The consequences range from a bad user experience to a prolonged outage. Harbourmaster eliminates that friction entirely. One command, six sources, one confident verdict.
Describe how you have used Coral in your:
Coral is not a supporting detail in Harbourmaster, it is the architecture. The entire product is only possible because of Coral's ability to JOIN multiple sources in a single SQL query.

The core query joins six sources simultaneously:
Harbourmaster executes one parameterized Coral SQL query that pulls from github.pull_requests and github.workflows (CI status and PR merge state), sentry.issues (current error rate versus the 24-hour baseline), datadog.monitors and datadog.metrics (infrastructure health and latency), pagerduty.incidents (whether a live incident is ongoing right now), statusgator.monitors (third-party dependency health — Stripe, Twilio, AWS), and linear.issues (whether all tickets scoped to this release milestone are closed). All six sources are joined in a single query, correlated by the current timestamp and the engineer's specified service and release parameters.

Why this matters: Without Coral, replicating this would require six separate authenticated HTTP clients, six sets of pagination logic, six different response schemas, and custom glue code to merge the results. That is not a one-day build but  a week of integration work. Coral reduces it to a single query and zero glue code, which is exactly what makes Harbourmaster feasible as a real tool.

At its core, the platform leverages a Python FastAPI backend powered by LangGraph and Gemini 3.5 Flash. Instead of running rigid scripts, the AI operates as an autonomous agent. When a user inputs a target, the agent dynamically reasons through the problem: it first triggers a native DNS resolution tool to convert URLs to IPv4 addresses, then autonomously pipes that data into the AbuseIPDB network to gather real-time threat telemetry, and finally compiles a comprehensive markdown security report.

When a user inputs a target, Coral analyzes the string. If it detects a domain name or URL (e.g., github.com), Coral autonomously decides to pause, trigger a backend Python DNS resolution tool to extract the underlying IPv4 address, and then carry that new data forward to the next step.

Project description:
Aletheia is a real-time agent reliability console that catches hallucinations and false claims before users do.

Agents make confident outputs — “the deploy succeeded,” “the API is healthy” — but those claims often conflict with what the runtime actually recorded. Aletheia closes that gap using Coral as an analytical reasoning engine, not just a data source.

Three Coral sources are joined in a multi-CTE evidence graph: agent outputs and tool calls, Sentry-style error logs, and Slack-style incident messages. Coral computes evidence density, contradiction dimensions, temporal windows, and a signal score entirely inside SQL — before the LLM ever gets involved. Only high-signal flagged outputs go to the judge model via TokenRouter.

The result is a verdict card for each flagged output showing risk level, confidence, affected users, contradiction dimensions, joined evidence, and recommended action.

Coral turns scattered operational data into a queryable evidence graph. Aletheia uses that graph to hold agents accountable to their own evidence.
Describe how you have used Coral in your:
Coral is the analytical core of Aletheia, not a wrapper around it.

I created three custom Coral sources: aletheia_agent (outputs and tool calls), aletheia_sentry (error logs), and aletheia_slack (incident messages). These are joined in a single multi-CTE SQL query that computes the full reliability matrix before any LLM inference happens.

The query structure:

WITH production_outputs AS (...),
     tool_rollup AS (...),
     error_rollup AS (...),
     incident_rollup AS (...),
     evidence_graph AS (...),
     contradiction_matrix AS (...)
SELECT * FROM ranked_reliability
WHERE coral_risk_level = 'HIGH'
ORDER BY coral_signal_score DESC;


Each CTE is a reasoning step. By the time the query returns, Coral has computed temporal_window_10m (did errors occur within 10 minutes of the agent claim), evidence_density (how much contradicting signal exists across sources), contradiction_dimensions (which conflict flags fired — rollback, safety, health, escalation), and coral_signal_score (the final ranked reliability matrix).

The judge LLM only explains what Coral already determined. That separation — Coral as the evidence engine, LLM as the explainer — is the core architectural decision Aletheia is built around.
How was your hackathon experience?:
Coral surprised me. I came in planning to use it as a data layer. I left having built an analytical reasoning engine inside SQL — the multi-CTE evidence graph wasn’t in my original plan, Coral made it possible.

The learning curve was real but fast. Getting cross-source JOINs running cleanly and making Coral’s signal score drive LLM triage was exactly the kind of infrastructure work you don’t get from tutorials.

Aletheia is also directly connected to research I’m pursuing on real-time agent reliability detection. This hackathon gave me a working proof of concept in 24 hours. Best possible outcome.

Project description:
Software bugs don't die when you close them. They wait. The Forgotten Prophet is a Python agent that proves it by JOINing GitHub's closed issues, Sentry's ignored errors, and Slack's deleted messages in one Coral SQL query, then scoring each ghost on a 0–100 Haunting Scale based on how quickly the "won't fix" became a production incident.
The core insight is architectural: Coral eliminates 500 lines of glue code that would otherwise stitch three APIs together in Python. DATEDIFF does the time math in SQL. A custom Coral source (slack-export.coral.yaml) surfaces deleted Slack messages — forensic evidence that standard connectors can't see. Groq's LLaMA 3.3 70B reads only the final 8 rows, never raw payloads, and generates a structured Ghost Report. For every ghost scoring 80+, a GitHub issue is auto-created. For every ghost scoring 70+, a Slack DM is sent to the original closer. The full report posts to #incidents with links.
Six ghosts found. Four critical. Top score: 100/100  three days between "won't fix" and the P0 it became. The intelligence is in the SQL.
Describe how you have used Coral in your:
Coral is the entire engine of The Forgotten Prophet — not a wrapper around it.
Most agents built for this hackathon will use an LLM to fetch data from GitHub, Sentry, and Slack separately, stuff the raw API responses into a context window, and ask the model to find patterns. That approach burns tokens, hallucinates correlations, and produces non-deterministic scores.
The Forgotten Prophet inverts this completely.
Coral executes a single cross-source SQL JOIN across three live APIs
What Coral specifically handles:

Cross-source JOIN — GitHub closed issues joined with Sentry fatal errors on keyword match, then LEFT JOINed with Slack archived threads on thread reference. Zero glue code.
Auth below deck — GitHub OAuth, Sentry API key, Slack Bot Token all handled inside Coral. The agent never manages auth.
DATEDIFF across APIs — DATEDIFF('day', github.closed_at, sentry.first_seen) computes the exact number of days between "won't fix" and the fatal production error it became. This column is computed inside Coral across two live APIs. No ETL. No warehouse.
Haunting Score in SQL — The 0–100 score formula (LEAST(100, reopen_signal + sentry_depth + slack_ghost)) is computed deterministically inside Coral — not by the LLM. The LLM receives the pre-scored result, never raw API data.
Custom Source (Bounty) — We ship slack-export.coral.yaml, a custom Coral source that exposes Slack's deleted and archived messages as a SQL table. Standard Slack MCP only surfaces live messages. Our source surfaces the ghost data — the unresolved "but what if…" threads where engineers saw the problem coming but nobody answered. This is the third signal in the Haunting Score formula.

The result: Coral returns 5–8 compact rows. Groq/LLaMA reads those rows and writes the Ghost Report. The LLM never sees raw GitHub, Sentry, or Slack API responses. The intelligence — the JOIN, the correlation, the score — lives entirely in the SQL.

Project description:
CoralOps is an Autonomous Release Intelligence and Guardian platform designed to protect production environments from bad feature flag rollouts.

The Problem:
While feature flags allow teams to release code fast, verifying the safety of a rollout is a fragmented, manual process. To decide if a flag toggle is safe, developers must become a    
"human JOIN"—spending 30+ minutes manually checking Sentry for error spikes, GitHub for PR sizes, PagerDuty for on-call alerts, and Statuspage for cloud infrastructure outages. Under   
pressure, these checks are often skipped, resulting in extended production incidents.

The Solution:
CoralOps eliminates this bottleneck by using the Coral SQL engine to treat these 5 separate live SaaS APIs as standard relational tables. When a rollout or trigger occurs, CoralOps     
executes a single federated SQL JOIN across all platforms in just ~35 milliseconds.

Our deterministic scoring engine rates the release risk from 0 to 100 based on 8 weighted operational signals (such as PR additions, incident status, and error frequency). The telemetry
is fed to a Groq Llama-3.3 LLM to generate an instant, plain-English risk report. If the score exceeds 80, CoralOps acts autonomously in under 3 seconds—reverting the risky flag via the
LaunchDarkly REST API, dispatching a Slack alert, and saving the full audit trail to a local PostgreSQL database with index-optimized ULIDs.

With CoralOps, manual cross-platform correlation is reduced to an autonomous closed-loop rollback, guaranteeing absolute stability with zero customer impact.

Tech Stack:
Coral SQL, React 19, Node.js, Express, TypeScript, PostgreSQL, Prisma, Groq Llama 3.3, LaunchDarkly, GitHub, PagerDuty, Sentry, and Slack APIs.
Describe how you have used Coral in your:
Coral is the absolute core of CoralOps. Without Coral, building this project would have required writing thousands of lines of complex, brittle glue code to coordinate separate REST    
APIs, manage five different OAuth/token authentications, orchestrate custom rate limiters, handle paginated payloads, and normalize varying JSON structures. Coral reduces all of this to a single queryable database abstraction.

Here is exactly how Coral is utilized in CoralOps:

1. Unified Data Federation Layer:
Coral allows us to treat 5 highly disparate live SaaS platforms (LaunchDarkly, GitHub, PagerDuty, Sentry, and Statuspage.io) as standard virtual database tables.
2. Federated SQL JOIN Querying:
When a safety check is triggered, the Express backend uses a local CLI bridge to execute a single, federated SQL statement that joins all five platforms simultaneously:

• Queries 'launchdarkly.flag_environments' to check the target flag status.
• LEFT JOINs 'github.pulls' to inspect change size and merge times.
• LEFT JOINs 'pagerduty.incidents' to capture unresolved on-call alerts.
• LEFT JOINs 'sentry.issues' to detect active runtime exceptions.
• LEFT JOINs 'statuspage.incidents' to evaluate cloud infrastructure health.

Current LLMs are fundamentally limited by context. When used as personal 
assistants, they fail because they cannot fetch, remember, or cross-reference 
the actual data you generate every day. I built Abra to fix this context gap.

Abra is a sovereign, voice-first Life OS that treats your entire existence

Notion task completion drops to Strava fatigue scores, or correlating Voice 
Diary mood signals with Chess.com blitz rating trends. I built two DSL v3 
source specs from scratch: chesscom.yml (public API, 4 tables) and 
strava.yml (OAuth 2.0 + PKCE, 3 tables).

Because Abra sits on top of this live matrix, it generates a 
hyper-personalized morning briefing every day and powers a chat terminal 
where you can ask anything about your life and get a hallucination-free, 
data-backed answer.

The backend is FastAPI with a fail-fast LLM orchestration layer 
(Gemini → Groq → OpenRouter) that auto-truncates payloads and reroutes 
instantly on rate limits. Visualized through a dark-mode React HUD tracking 
cross-domain trends in real-time.

Abra isn't a chatbot. It's an autonomous engine that finally gives an LLM 
the real-world context it needs to be genuinely useful.

Coral is the foundational data engine that solves Abra's LLM context problem. 
Instead of brittle ETL pipelines or hundreds of lines of Python parsing

1. Custom Source Specs: I authored two DSL v3 Coral YAML specifications from 
scratch — chesscom.yml mapping the Chess.com public API into 4 SQL tables

Project description:
# 🚀 Inspiration

Engineering teams spend a huge amount of time jumping between tools just to understand what's happening in a project. A developer might need to check GitHub for pull requests, Linear for sprint tasks, Sentry for production errors, and SonarQube for code quality before making a decision.

We asked ourselves a simple question:

**What if engineers could talk to their entire engineering stack through one intelligent assistant instead of opening multiple dashboards?**

That's how **CoralOps** was born — an Enterprise Intelligence Agent powered by Coral and MCP that brings all engineering data into a single conversational experience.

# 💡 What it does

CoralOps acts as a central AI assistant for engineering teams.

Instead of manually searching through multiple tools, users can ask questions in plain English such as:

* "Are there any critical bugs blocking this sprint?"
* "Which open pull requests have low test coverage?"
* "Show me unresolved production issues related to this feature."

The agent understands the request, gathers live information from multiple systems, and returns a single, actionable answer.

Using **Model Context Protocol (MCP)** and **Turbot Coral**, CoralOps translates natural language into federated SQL queries that can retrieve and combine data across GitHub, Linear, Sentry, and SonarQube in real time.

# 🛠️ How we built it

### Frontend

* Next.js + TypeScript
* Tailwind CSS
* Deployed on Vercel

### Backend

* Java 17
* Spring Boot
* Spring AI
* Deployed on Render

### AI Layer

* Llama 3.3 70B Versatile
* Powered by Groq for ultra-fast inference

### Data & MCP Layer

* Turbot Coral CLI as the federated SQL engine
* MCP for structured tool access across multiple platforms

### Custom SonarQube Integration

One of the things we're most proud of is integrating **SonarQube as a custom external source**.

Rather than treating SonarQube as a separate dashboard, we configured it directly within Coral using YAML-based source definitions and securely connected it to our SonarQube server. This allowed Coral to expose SonarQube metrics as queryable tables alongside GitHub, Linear, and Sentry data.

As a result, the AI can answer questions involving:

* Code coverage
* Security hotspots
* Code smells
* Quality gate status
* Reliability and maintainability metrics

all using the same federated SQL workflow.

# 🚧 Challenges we ran into

Getting the entire AI stack running reliably in a cloud environment was our biggest challenge.

Coral CLI depends on native Linux libraries and initializes a local database engine at startup. When deploying on Render's free tier, we encountered memory pressure, startup delays, and timeout issues between Spring AI and the MCP layer.

To solve this, we:

* Tuned JVM memory limits with `-Xmx200m`
* Migrated to Ubuntu 24.04
* Customized our Docker setup
* Built startup scripts to pre-initialize Coral schemas
* Automated loading of external sources, including our SonarQube YAML configuration, before MCP connections were established

These optimizations significantly improved startup reliability and overall performance.

# 🎉 Accomplishments we're proud of

* Built a practical enterprise use case using the emerging Model Context Protocol (MCP).
* Successfully configured SonarQube as a custom external source through YAML-based integration.
* Enabled AI-driven federated SQL queries across GitHub, Linear, Sentry, and SonarQube.
* Demonstrated that an LLM can correlate data across multiple engineering platforms to provide meaningful operational insights.
* Overcame complex deployment and infrastructure challenges to deliver a fully cloud-hosted, production-ready solution.

CoralOps shows how AI can move beyond simple chat interfaces and become a true engineering teammate with real-time access to an organization's operational knowledge.
Describe how you have used Coral in your:
We utilized Turbot Coral as the core federated data layer and primary "brain" for our Enterprise Intelligence Agent. Instead of writing custom API integration glue code for every single SaaS tool, we deployed the Coral CLI to act as a unified, local-first SQL runtime.

Specifically, we integrated Coral using the Model Context Protocol (MCP) via Spring AI on our Java backend. By wrapping Coral in an MCP server, we were able to natively expose four distinct SaaS APIs (GitHub, Linear, Sentry, and a custom SonarQube external source) directly to our LLM (Llama 3.3).

When a user asks a question in our conversational UI (e.g., "What are the open linear issues?"), Coral enables the LLM to write standard, deterministic SQL queries. Coral intercepts this SQL, translates it into the necessary REST API calls in the background, handles the pagination and authentication, and returns the tabular data back to the agent. We even wrote a custom Bash wrapper script to dynamically mount and authenticate Coral's schemas at runtime within our Docker container, ensuring the federated SQL layer works seamlessly in the cloud.

Project description:
SprintLens is an AI-powered engineering intelligence platform that transforms fragmented engineering data into actionable sprint insights in a single command. Built around Coral's cross-source SQL runtime, SprintLens joins data from GitHub, Linear, Sentry, PagerDuty, and Slack locally on the user's machine, creating a unified view of engineering performance without requiring a backend, dashboard, or centralized data warehouse.

At its core, SprintLens follows a simple principle: engineering managers should spend time solving problems, not collecting data. Instead of manually switching between tools to understand sprint health, SprintLens automatically correlates delivery metrics, operational signals, and team workload to surface meaningful insights.

The Role of Coral

SprintLens is powered by Coral, a local cross-source SQL engine that enables SQL queries across multiple SaaS platforms simultaneously. Coral acts as the data layer, allowing SprintLens to perform joins between engineering systems that normally operate in isolation.

Using Coral, SprintLens can answer questions such as:

Which stale pull requests are correlated with production incidents?
Which engineers have high workload across issues, PRs, and on-call pages?
How do deployment frequency and lead time compare against DORA benchmarks?
Which bottlenecks are slowing team velocity?

Because all queries execute locally, organizations retain control over their data while gaining unified visibility across engineering workflows.

The Role of Claude and LLM Reasoning

SprintLens deliberately separates data collection from reasoning.

Coral gathers structured facts, metrics, and correlations. Claude then acts as an engineering analyst, interpreting those facts to identify:

Root causes behind slow delivery
Review bottlenecks
Burnout risks
Incident-prone changes
Actionable recommendations for managers

Rather than generating reports directly from raw tool data, Claude receives curated engineering signals and produces concise, human-readable briefings tailored for managers, executives, or individual contributors. This architecture ensures that AI focuses on interpretation while Coral remains the source of truth for data retrieval.

DORA Metrics as a First-Class Feature

A key capability of SprintLens is automated DORA (DevOps Research and Assessment) metric analysis. The platform calculates industry-standard engineering performance indicators directly from engineering activity:

Deployment Frequency
Lead Time for Changes
Change Failure Rate
Mean Time to Recovery (MTTR)

SprintLens automatically classifies teams into Elite, High, Medium, or Low performance tiers using established DORA benchmarks, providing an objective measure of engineering effectiveness. Unlike narrative reports, DORA calculations are generated deterministically from Coral query results and do not require an LLM.

Core Design Principles

SprintLens is built around four guiding principles:

Local First
All data collection and correlation happen on the user's machine. There is no SprintLens server and no centralized storage.
Cross-Source Intelligence
Insights emerge by connecting signals across GitHub, Linear, Sentry, PagerDuty, and Slack rather than analyzing each tool independently.
Facts Before AI
Coral produces structured engineering facts first; Claude reasons only over validated signals rather than raw datasets.
Actionable Outcomes
Every report is designed to answer practical management questions about velocity, workload, risk, and operational health, not just display metrics.
Describe how you have used Coral in your:
SprintLens uses Coral as its core data layer, allowing us to query and join data across GitHub, Linear, Sentry, PagerDuty, and Slack using SQL. Instead of building custom integrations and data pipelines, Coral provides a unified view of engineering activity across tools.

We use Coral to:

- Compute DORA metrics (Deployment Frequency, Lead Time, Change Failure Rate, and MTTR)
- Correlate PRs, incidents, errors, and workload across multiple systems

Project description:
LLM Wall is an open-source security proxy that sits between an organization's applications and LLM providers (OpenAI, Ollama, Gemini, NVIDIA). Every prompt is inspected by a multi-agent security engine before it reaches the provider, preventing prompt injection, jailbreaking, and data exfiltration.

Coral Integration (Track 1: Enterprise Agent)

Coral is integrated as the core investigative layer across five subsystems:

1. IncidentInvestigator — Subscribes to the A2A threat bus. On every threat detection/block event, it runs 5 parallel Coral SQL queries across GitHub (PRs), Sentry (errors), Slack (incidents), PagerDuty (triggers), and Datadog (anomalies). Results are stored on an immutable blockchain ledger for audit trail integrity.

2. PatternHunter — Queries the organization's actual GitHub repos, Notion docs, and Slack channels via Coral SQL to find exposed prompts, internal terminology, and API key patterns. Uses an LLM to synthesize targeted regex patterns that are hot-reloaded into the Guardian security engine — detection patterns that evolve with the org.

3. Honeypot Generator — Reads real org data (private repo names, issue titles) through Coral, then generates deceptive decoy prompts that look like legitimate internal requests. Unique strings from each honeypot are registered as Sentinel IOCs — any request containing them is instantly flagged, catching attackers who probe with org-specific knowledge.

4. Policy Generator — Queries Notion (security policies), Confluence (runbooks), and GitHub (incident reports) via Coral to understand the organization's security posture. An LLM then suggests optimal Guardian thresholds, critical threat categories, allowed providers, and fidelity rules — security policy informed by actual docs.

5. MCP Tools — Three Model Context Protocol tools registered in the MCP broker: coral_sql (ad-hoc SQL), coral_list_catalog (discover tables/schemas), and coral_search_catalog (full-text search), enabling any MCP client to query Coral sources.
Describe how you have used Coral in your:
Coral runs as a local CLI binary that speaks SQL to APIs and databases — no cloud dependency, no data leaving the network. The project wraps it in an async Python subprocess layer (CoralEngine) and points it at five subsystems:

1. Schema-Aware Query Filtering  
Instead of hardcoding table names and praying they exist, every Coral query first runs SELECT DISTINCT schema_name FROM coral.tables. If a schema like github or sentry isn't registered, the system skips the query entirely — no "table not found" noise, no wasted seconds on a subprocess that will fail. This dropped investigation latency from 11 seconds to 2.4 seconds in the dev environment.

2. Five Cross-Source Threat Queries in Parallel  
When a threat gets detected or blocked, IncidentInvestigator fans out 5 Coral SQL queries concurrently via asyncio.gather — GitHub pull requests merged in the last 24h, Sentry fatal errors from the last 6h, Slack messages from #incidents and #security, PagerDuty triggered incidents, Datadog active anomalies. Each query has a per-query timeout so one hanging source can't stall the whole investigation. Results land on a blockchain ledger block — tamper-proof, timestamped, chained.

3. Pattern Synthesis from Org Data  
PatternHunter runs Coral SQL against github.repos, github.issue_comments, notion.pages, and slack.messages. The returned rows — real repo descriptions, real issue bodies, real Slack threads — get fed into an LLM with a strict JSON schema prompt. The LLM spits back regex patterns for the Guardian engine. No placebos, no mock data. If the source isn't configured, Coral's empty result set means zero queries run.

4. Honeypots That Know Your Org  
The Honeypot Generator uses Coral to pull private repo names and issue titles, then an LLM weaves them into decoy prompts that sound exactly like internal requests. The unique strings become Sentinel IOCs. An attacker probing with org-specific knowledge hits a honeypot instantly.

5. Policy Informed by Actual Docs  
Policy Generator runs Coral SQL against notion.pages (security policies), confluence.pages (runbooks), and github.issues (incident reports). The returned text gets summarized by an LLM into threshold recommendations — block at 75, quarantine at 50, these three threat categories should always block. No guesswork.

6. MCP Tools  
Three MCP tools (coral_sql, coral_list_catalog, coral_search_catalog) let any MCP client run ad-hoc Coral queries or browse the catalog at runtime. The broker just shells out to the same CoralEngine underneath.
How was your hackathon experience?:
Honestly it was a blast but also exhausting. I went in thinking I'd just bolt Coral onto an existing project and call it a day. Turned into a full rewrite of how my security proxy investigates threats. Coral's SQL approach is deceptively simple on the surface — SELECT * FROM github.issues — but wiring it into five async subsystems, handling every edge case where sources aren't configured, getting the blockchain ledger to play nice, all while making sure the whole thing doesn't crash when a single query times out... that took way longer than I expected.
The best part was seeing that first investigation report land on the chain with real data from Coral. The worst part was debugging why coral.tables returns different schemas depending on what sources are installed. Would I do it again? Absolutely. Just maybe with more sleep.

Describe how you have used Coral in your:
Coral is the entire data foundation of FreightSense — not a peripheral 
integration but the core architectural layer that makes the project possible.

1. CROSS-SOURCE SQL JOINS
The centerpiece of FreightSense is a three-source JOIN that runs in a 
single Coral SQL query:

SELECT pd.title, pd.urgency, li.identifier, li.title AS investigation,
       se.title AS system_error, se.level
FROM pagerduty.incidents pd
LEFT JOIN linear.issues li 
  ON li.team_key = 'JEF' AND li.state_type != 'completed'
LEFT JOIN sentry.issues se 
  ON se.status = 'unresolved' AND se.level IN ('error', 'fatal')
WHERE pd.status IN ('triggered', 'acknowledged')
ORDER BY pd.created_at DESC

Without Coral, this would require three separate API clients, custom 
pagination logic for each, manual auth handling, and Python code to 
stitch the results together. With Coral, it is one SQL statement. 
Data stays local — nothing leaves the machine.

2. FIVE SOURCES CONNECTED
All five sources were connected using coral source add --interactive:
- pagerduty: incidents, services, oncalls, escalation policies
- sentry: issues, events, projects
- linear: issues, cycles, teams, users
- github: pulls, repos, commits, workflows  
- slack: channels, users

3. THREE PROVEN QUERIES
FreightSense runs three pre-built Coral SQL queries:
- risk_intelligence.sql: PagerDuty + Linear + Sentry
- pipeline_health.sql: Sentry + Linear
- sprint_status.sql: Linear + PagerDuty + Sentry

Each query was discovered and tested using coral sql --format json 
before being integrated into the FastAPI backend.

4. SCHEMA DISCOVERY WORKFLOW
Following the Coral skills workflow, every table and column name was 
discovered using coral.tables and coral.columns before writing a 
single JOIN. This prevented all column name errors and made the 
queries reliable first time.

5. AI AGENT TOOL
The Groq-powered AI agent uses Coral as its primary tool. When a user 
asks a natural language question, the agent calls run_coral_query(sql) 
which executes coral sql --format json via subprocess, returns the 
JSON rows, and feeds them back to the model for analysis. The agent 
never guesses — it always queries Coral first.

6. MCP INTEGRATION
Coral is wired into the development environment via mcp.json with 
coral mcp-stdio, and Coral skills were installed via 
npx skills add withcoral/skills to teach the AI agent the 
correct schema-discovery-first workflow.

The key insight Coral gave me: AI agents should not be plumbing 
engineers. They should be analysts. Coral handles the plumbing —

Project description:
War Room is an AI-powered incident intelligence and operations copilot. I built it to help engineering teams investigate incidents by correlating evidence from tools like GitHub, Slack, Sentry, Datadog, Linear, Jira, PagerDuty, Grafana, and more, with Coral as the central query and evidence layer.

1. Tech Stack

Frontend: Next.js, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui, React Query  
Backend: FastAPI, Python, LangChain/LangGraph-style orchestration, LiteLLM  
Data/Auth: Supabase Auth, PostgreSQL, Prisma, organization/project membership model, RLS policies  
Monorepo: Turborepo-style structure with `apps/web`, `apps/api`, `packages/*`, and `services/*`  
Core integration layer: Coral CLI/MCP, Coral SQL, project-scoped Coral source config

2. What It Is And What It Does

War Room helps teams move from “something is broken” to “here is the likely cause, evidence, timeline, confidence, and next action.”

It supports incident intake (webhook and manual), investigation timelines, AI root-cause analysis, evidence citation, remediation suggestions, Slack coordination, postmortems, reports, and project-level operational configuration. The main idea is that every AI conclusion should be auditable, so the app shows Coral SQL, source tables, confidence scores, evidence, and reasoning instead of hiding everything behind a black-box chatbot.

3. How It Works

A user configures a project and connects operational sources. Coral installs and tests project-scoped sources, exposes tables and War Room runs read-only Coral SQL across them.

For example, in an incident, War Room can correlate a GitHub deployment, Sentry error spike, Datadog latency increase, and Slack escalation thread. The result becomes part of the incident record as evidence, timeline context, Coral query metadata, and AI reasoning input. The explainability layer then uses Coral query coverage as part of the confidence calculation and citation chain.

4. Configurable Options

Coral-backed integrations:
GitHub, Slack, Sentry, Datadog, Linear, Jira, Notion, PagerDuty, Grafana, and LaunchDarkly. Each source has project-scoped credentials/config, encrypted secrets, Coral install/test status, table count, and readiness output.

Webhook and trigger configuration:
Webhook-capable providers include GitHub, Sentry, Datadog, Grafana, and PagerDuty. Webhooks support enabled/disabled state, encrypted verification secrets, last-rotated metadata, and verification modes like shared header/bearer, Sentry signature, Datadog header, Grafana HMAC, and PagerDuty signature. Trigger policies can configure provider, source type (poll or webhook), source reference, dedupe window, minimum confidence, required signals, severity mapping, service mapping, and Slack notification handoff.

BYOK AI model configuration:
Organizations can configure Google Gemini, OpenAI, or Anthropic models using LiteLLM-style model names. Supported presets include Gemini Flash/Pro models, OpenAI GPT-5/GPT-5 mini/GPT-4.1/GPT-4o, and Anthropic Claude models. API keys are encrypted, models can be tested, and only one model is enabled per organization for incident reasoning and generated artifacts.

Notifications configuration:
Notifications are sent via Slack; supports OAuth setup, channel sync, selected channels for incident notifications, AI updates, and war-room activity, plus notification/workflow toggles.

Ticket workflow configuration:
When Jira and Linear are both connected, the project can choose a default ticket provider for human-approved incident follow-ups.

5. Extras

The onboarding flow helps set up organization, project, services, integrations, webhooks, and optional BYOK AI models. The organization schema supports organizations, users, organization memberships, projects, project memberships, project integrations, AI model configs, services, incidents, trigger policies, and trigger events. RLS policies protect project trigger policies and trigger events so only authenticated project or organization members can read or write scoped operational data.

TL;DR:
I used Coral as the data access and correlation layer for War Room. Instead of treating tools as disconnected integrations, I use Coral sources and Coral SQL to query them through a common operational interface. In the project, Coral helps connect incident evidence across systems, preserve the exact SQL used for investigation, and make AI-generated conclusions auditable for technical reviewers and on-call engineers.


In War Room, I used Coral to power the incident investigation flow. The project is an AI operational intelligence platform, so the goal was not just to show alerts or chat with an LLM, but to let an engineer understand why an incident happened, what evidence supports the conclusion, and what action should happen next.

The Coral flow starts in the project integrations layer. A user connects sources such as GitHub, Slack, Sentry, Datadog, Linear, Jira, PagerDuty, etc as present in the UI. For each supported provider, the app stores the project-scoped integration config, encrypts secrets, installs/tests the Coral source, and checks whether Coral exposes catalog tables for that source.

When an investigation runs, War Room builds Coral SQL queries against those source tables. One example flow is a checkout latency incident where War Room correlates GitHub deployment data, Sentry issue spikes, Datadog latency metrics, and Slack incident discussion. Coral lets me express that as auditable SQL, such as joining deployment windows with error events and incident-channel messages. The SQL is intentionally visible in the UI so judges and users can inspect exactly what data path supported the AI conclusion (although it won't make sense to have this on by default if this were an actual product, just in interest of abstraction, but definitely visible if the users so wish).

The result is not just raw rows: the project also builds query context from the SQL, including source systems, tables, joins, and reasoning text explaining whether Coral is querying one source or correlating multiple sources.

The incident model stores Coral query metadata alongside the investigation: query id, title, SQL, touched tables, status, row count/error state, and execution context. That metadata is then used by the explainability layer. Coral query coverage contributes to confidence scoring, citations, causal-chain construction, and uncertainty reporting. This means the AI root-cause analysis can point back to concrete evidence like “this conclusion is supported by a Coral query touching github.pulls, sentry.issues, and slack.messages,” instead of producing an opaque answer.

Project description:
fathomOS is an incident forensics workspace and operational IDE designed for SREs ("Cursor for SREs"). 

During critical SEV-1 outages, engineers suffer from severe cognitive overload, manually acting as human JOIN tables by flipping between Datadog, Sentry, PagerDuty, and cloud status pages to build a timeline of events. fathomOS fundamentally re-architects this workflow. Instead of a passive, black-box AI chatbot that outputs unverifiable markdown summaries, fathomOS unifies infrastructure alerts, application exception logs, and performance metrics into a dense, interactive, multi-source relational grid. 

Featuring a persistent execution log, an integrated SQL editor for manual query override, and an active self-healing layer, fathomOS acts as a high-fidelity control tower that cuts mean time to resolution (MTTR) and automates blameless post-mortem timeline reconstruction from days to seconds.
Describe how you have used Coral in your:
fathomOS uses Coral SQL entirely locally as an ephemeral, federated micro-data warehouse to break down data silos across production tooling. 

Instead of forcing a cold LLM to generate massive, brittle 5-way SQL JOINs that predictably break under real-world API rate limits or schema variations, fathomOS implements an intelligent, multi-stage pipeline utilizing Coral as the core engine:

1. Stage 1 (Deterministic Seed): The system executes a highly optimized Coral query against `sentry.issues` to isolate the blast radius anchor for a degraded microservice.
2. Bounded Temporal Windowing: The Python backend intercepts these rows, extracts the localized service context, and calculates absolute chronological boundaries (min_ts and max_ts).
3. Downstream Federation: These exact parameters are passed back to target downstream Coral tables (`pagerduty.incidents`, `datadog.metrics`, `statusgator.outages`) in parallel, bounded execution streams.
4. Self-Healing Middleware: Every query passes through an autonomous correction loop. If a query hits a schema error or API constraint pushdown failure, our backend intercepts the runtime traceback, consults the Coral schema definition rules, and self-corrects the SQL mid-flight before rendering the data layers into structured visual components.

Coral turned raw, deeply nested REST APIs into a clean relational abstraction layer, allowing fathomOS to achieve zero-ETL, low-latency multi-source engineering forensics entirely on the operator's machine.

Enhanced the community Gmail source for Coral (withcoral/coral) using a declarative source specification (manifest.yaml and README only), not a separate application or engine changes.

The README documents Google OAuth desktop setup, Gmail API quota (including 20 units per messages.get), a two-step workflow (list or search for message ids, then fetch metadata for one id at a time), and why SQL joins into message_details are not supported when message_id is a required HTTP filter. Describe how you have used Coral in your:
Coral is the platform I contributed to, not a separate app I built on top of it. Coral turns external APIs into SQL-queryable sources so agents and developers can run queries locally. For this project I extended Coral’s community Gmail source by authoring a source specification: a manifest that declares how Coral should call the Gmail REST API, plus a README for setup and usage.

I used Coral’s source-spec workflow end to end. I defined new surfaces in the manifest (a search_messages function with kind search that maps to Gmail’s messages.list search parameter, and a message_details table that maps to messages.get with format=metadata for From, Subject, and Date). I validated the spec with make lint-sources and coral source lint, then installed and tested it with coral source add --interactive and coral source test gmail. I ran real queries with coral sql to prove search_messages returns message ids and message_details returns headers when message_id is provided as a literal filter, which matches how Coral executes required HTTP filters.

I also used Coral’s catalog and test-query model: the manifest includes test_queries that run automatically during source add and source test, so Coral verifies profile, messages, labels, table functions, and search in one flow. The documentation I wrote explains Coral-specific behavior, including the two-step pattern (discover ids with search or list, then fetch one message’s metadata) because Coral cannot push join-derived values into message_details’ required message_id filter.
