Project description:
Blast Radius is an AI incident analyst that automates the worst part of being
on-call: correlating across five different SaaS dashboards to figure out what
actually caused an incident.
When a feature flag flips, a deploy ships, or a metric spikes, a webhook fires
into our system and a Gemini-powered agent runs a multi-turn investigation
across LaunchDarkly, Sentry, and Vercel — all queried as a single federated
SQL database through Coral. The agent follows a discovery-first workflow
(catalog → plan → query → segment → verdict), produces a structured,
confidence-scored verdict, and the dashboard updates live via Supabase
Realtime within ~60 seconds.
The verdict tells you what caused the incident (flag, deploy, both, neither,
or inconclusive), how confident the system is, which sources were federated,
and the exact SQL queries the agent wrote — so every conclusion is
reproducible and auditable.
Stack: TypeScript end to end. Hono webhook API, BullMQ + Upstash Redis job
queue, Gemini 2.5 Flash agent loop over MCP, Coral as the SQL federation
layer, Supabase Postgres + Realtime + Storage for persistence and live
updates, React + Vite + lucide-react on the frontend, OpenTelemetry for
observability, multi-stage Docker, deployed on Cloud Run + Vercel.
We replace 15–30 minutes of frantic tab-hopping with one button click and a
verdict in a minute.
Describe how you have used Coral in your:
Coral is the single most important piece of our architecture — without it,
Blast Radius is not possible. Here is how we use it, end to end.

1. Coral runs as a sidecar inside the worker container

Our worker process spawns the Coral CLI as a child process and talks to it
over MCP (stdio transport) using @modelcontextprotocol/sdk. The container's
entrypoint script provisions every source from environment variables at boot
with `coral source add launchdarkly --yes`, `coral source add sentry --yes`,
and `coral source add --file sources/vercel.yaml --yes`. Credentials never
hit the source code or image — they live in env vars and end up only in
Coral's local store.

2. Five MCP tools exposed to the Gemini agent

We register list_catalog, list_columns, describe_table, sql, and feedback as
function declarations for Gemini. The agent never gets to write SQL until it
has called list_catalog and list_columns first — this discovery-first
workflow is baked into our system prompt and is exactly what Coral's docs
recommend. It eliminates an entire class of hallucinated-column-name errors.

3. Real cross-source federated SQL is the entire point

Our verdict comes from a single SQL JOIN that Coral executes across three
different APIs simultaneously. A representative query the agent writes at
runtime:

  SELECT
    ld.name        AS flag_name,
    ld.date        AS flag_flip_time,
    s.title        AS sentry_error,
    s.first_seen   AS error_first_seen,
    v.uid          AS deploy_id,
    v.created_at   AS deploy_time
  FROM launchdarkly.audit_log ld
  LEFT JOIN sentry.issues s
    ON s.first_seen > to_timestamp_millis(ld.date)
    AND s.first_seen < to_timestamp_millis(ld.date) + INTERVAL '30 minutes'
  LEFT JOIN vercel.deployments v
    ON v.created_at BETWEEN ld.date - 1800000 AND ld.date + 1800000
  WHERE ld.kind = 'flag'
    AND ld."from" = '<computed_epoch_ms>'
    AND ld."to"   = '<computed_epoch_ms>'
  ORDER BY ld.date DESC

Coral federates this across LaunchDarkly's REST API and Sentry's REST API
and Vercel's REST API transparently, handling auth, pagination, and rate
limits below deck. Without Coral, we would be writing three separate API
clients, three different pagination loops, three different auth flows, and
joining the results in JavaScript — and the agent would burn its entire
context window on raw JSON before it could correlate anything.

4. A custom Vercel source spec to fill a gap

LaunchDarkly and Sentry are bundled with Coral. Vercel is not. We wrote
sources/vercel.yaml — a custom source spec using HeaderAuth, cursor
pagination on Vercel's /v6/deployments endpoint, and format_timestamp:
unix_ms — to add vercel.deployments as a first-class Coral table. This is
what makes our "flag vs. deploy" causal logic possible: when the agent sees
a flag flip with no deploy in the same window, it can confidently attribute
the incident to the flag. We are also submitting this spec to the Source
Spec bounty.

5. --enable-feedback for graceful failures

We launch Coral with `coral mcp-stdio --enable-feedback` so when the agent
gets stuck (a column that doesn't exist, a required filter it doesn't know
about), it calls the feedback tool instead of looping forever. Every report
is logged locally and surfaces in our internal logs.

6. Every query is persisted as evidence

The agent loop has an onQuery callback. Every time the agent calls the sql
tool, the worker inserts a row into the query_runs table with the exact SQL
and uploads the result JSON to Supabase Storage. The investigation detail
page in the dashboard shows the literal SQL the agent wrote and a link to
the row-level result snapshot. Every verdict is fully reproducible months
later — point at the snapshot, replay the query.

7. A health-check loop keeps source status live

A repeatable BullMQ job runs every 5 minutes and calls list_tables on each
source through Coral. The result upserts to a sources table, which powers
the live green/amber/red status dots on the Sources page in the UI. Source
outages become observable, not silent.

8. OpenTelemetry to prove the efficiency story

Our worker exports OTel traces with custom span attributes:
analysis.sql_query_count, analysis.sources_used, analysis.duration_ms,
analysis.cause_label, analysis.confidence. Coral's own OTLP traces export
to the same collector. The result: a single trace per analysis showing
every federated SQL Coral ran, its latency, and its row count.
Why this matters
Without Coral, every analysis would mean the agent making N separate API
calls, stuffing N walls of raw JSON into its context, and trying to do
temporal correlation in its head. That is exactly the multi-tool, high-
post-processing failure mode Coral's own benchmark shows agents lose at.
With Coral, the JOIN happens locally inside DataFusion before the model
sees a single row. The agent gets tidy result sets, the verdict is causal
and confident, and the entire investigation finishes in 60–90 seconds.
Coral is not a library we imported. It is the read plane our agent runs on.
How was your hackathon experience?:
Genuinely one of the more focused weeks I've had this year. The constraint of
"all data is read through one SQL layer" forced us to rethink how agents
should actually consume data — instead of stuffing context windows with raw
JSON from five separate REST APIs, we let Coral do the federation locally
and gave the agent tidy result sets. That single design decision is what
made our analysis loop work in 60 seconds instead of timing out.

Highlights:
- Watching the first real cross-source JOIN return rows correlating a
  LaunchDarkly flag flip with a Sentry error timestamp was the most
  satisfying moment of the week.
- Coral's discovery-first workflow (list_catalog → list_columns → query) is
  genuinely the right pattern for agentic data access. We will use this
  shape on future projects whether or not we use Coral specifically.
- The MCP integration was clean. Spawning Coral as a stdio child process
  and connecting via @modelcontextprotocol/sdk took maybe 30 lines.
Things that took longer than expected:
- Schema discovery on day one. LaunchDarkly's audit_log requires `from`/`to`
  filters as epoch ms strings, and `kind = 'flag'` not `'featureFlag'`.
  Querying coral.columns first instead of guessing saved us hours later.
- LLM date math. Gemini was unreliable at computing epoch ms windows, so we
  pre-compute them in TypeScript and inject the exact values into the
  prompt. Eliminated an entire class of empty-result bugs.
What I would do differently:
- Start with the seed/curation data on day one, not day five. The backend
  was real well before the demo data was demo-able.
- Spend more time on the first 30 seconds of the dashboard. Judges decide
  fast and the technical depth is invisible if the landing experience is
  weak.
Huge thanks to the WeMakeDevs team and Coral for putting this together. The
$10k pool is generous and the side bounties (source spec, blog, swag) made
it feel rewarding even for things outside the main project. Would do again.

Project description:
Enterprise support teams spend 15–20 minutes per escalated ticket manually cross-referencing Intercom, Sentry, Slack, GitHub, and Linear to diagnose customer issues — five logins, five searches, five mental correlations. NEXUS automates this entirely.
The system executes one cross-source SQL JOIN across all five APIs via Coral Protocol, replacing five independent integrations with a single parameterized query. A sequential LangGraph pipeline of five agents processes the result: the Ticket Agent enriches state with SQLite history, the Coral Agent queries Coral for correlated signals, the Signal Agent transforms raw rows into typed Python dataclasses with explicit found: bool guards, the Synthesis Agent feeds all signals to Claude (claude-sonnet-4-6) to produce a Pydantic-validated TechnicalBrief, and the Dispatch Agent routes the diagnosis to Intercom and optionally Slack based on confidence thresholds. A React dashboard with Server-Sent Events provides real-time pipeline visibility.
Enterprise value: 30× faster diagnosis (30 seconds vs. 20 minutes), explainable AI with timestamped causal chains, and alert fatigue prevention through confidence-gated routing.
Coral status: Fully integrated with both live (Coral CLI) and demo (JSON fixtures) modes. In DEMO_MODE, deterministic mock data is used for reproducible demonstrations. Live mode requires the Coral CLI and configured data sources.
---

- Cross-Source SQL via Coral Protocol: Single parameterized query with 4 LEFT JOINs correlates Intercom, Sentry, Slack, GitHub, and Linear through Coral's unified data access layer — zero per-source API client code.
- Sequential Typed Agent Pipeline: Five LangGraph agents execute in strict order with typed NexusState and one-writer-per-key discipline, ensuring state is predictable and debuggable at every step.
- Null-Safe Signal Transformation: Raw Coral rows are converted to typed dataclasses with found: bool guards, preventing null values from reaching the LLM prompt and eliminating hallucination vectors.
- LLM Synthesis with Pydantic Validation: Claude output is parsed through TechnicalBrief Pydantic model with field validators for type coercion, empty-string-to-null conversion, retry on parse failure, and hardcoded JSON fallbacks.
- Confidence-Gated Dispatch Routing: Routing matrix checks confidence (threshold: 70%) and severity — high confidence posts only to Intercom, low confidence or critical severity escalates to Slack with Block Kit formatting.

Project description: NEXUS is an AI-powered engineering intelligence agent that answers any question about your engineering organisation in plain English — by executing cross-source Coral SQL queries across GitHub, Sentry, PagerDuty, Stripe, and 10+ live data sources simultaneously. It eliminates the 34-minute context-switching problem engineers face during incidents by joining data from multiple tools in a single query, delivering root cause analysis, DORA metrics, and pre-merge risk scores in under 30 seconds. Built for the Pirates of the Coral-bean Hackathon 2026 (Track 1: Enterprise Agent), NEXUS uses Gemini 2.0 Flash as its reasoning engine with a custom SSE streaming agentic loop and three original Coral source specs for Buildkite, Beehiiv, and Dub.
Describe how you have used Coral in your:
When I started building NEXUS, I had one core frustration in mind: every time something breaks in production, engineers waste 20–40 minutes just gathering context — opening GitHub to find the recent deploy, switching to Sentry to find the error, jumping to PagerDuty to check the incident timeline, and then trying to mentally stitch it all together. By the time you figure out what happened, you've already lost the most critical minutes of the incident.

Coral completely changes this. And it became the heart of everything I built.

The moment Coral clicked for me

The first time I wrote this query and watched it actually execute:


SELECT
  g.title AS deploy,
  g.merged_by AS author,
  s.error_message,
  s.users_affected,
  pd.urgency AS incident_severity
FROM github.pull_requests g
JOIN sentry.issues s
  ON s.first_seen BETWEEN g.merged_at AND g.merged_at + INTERVAL '2 hours'
JOIN pagerduty.incidents pd
  ON pd.created_at >= g.merged_at
WHERE s.level = 'fatal'
ORDER BY s.users_affected DESC
...and it returned rows joining three completely separate APIs — GitHub, Sentry, and PagerDuty — with zero glue code, I knew this was genuinely different. I didn't write any API clients. I didn't handle pagination. I didn't manage tokens in the query itself. Coral just handled all of it. That single query would have taken me a full day to replicate with raw API calls and still wouldn't have been as clean.

What I actually built with Coral

NEXUS is an AI agent that answers engineering questions in natural language. Under the hood, every answer is backed by a real Coral SQL query against live data. The architecture is simple: the user asks something, Gemini writes the SQL, Coral executes it, and the results come back as structured JSON that the agent reasons over.

I wrapped the Coral CLI in a Node.js function using spawnSync, exposed it as a tool called coral_query(sql) that the Gemini agent can call, and wired it into a streaming API route. The agent also has a get_schema() tool that runs SELECT schema_name, table_name FROM coral.tables so it can discover what sources are connected before writing queries. This means the agent is genuinely adaptive — if you add a new source to Coral, NEXUS automatically knows about it and can query it without any code changes.

I connected four live sources: GitHub (362 tables), PagerDuty (112 tables), Stripe (153 tables), and Sentry (12 tables) — 639 queryable tables total, all accessible through the same SQL interface.

The three features powered entirely by Coral

Incident War Room is the flagship feature. When you ask "what caused the production incident at 3 AM?", NEXUS runs a cross-source JOIN across GitHub pull requests, Sentry fatal errors, and PagerDuty incidents. It identifies the root cause commit, the number of affected users, and the revenue impact — all from one query. What used to take 30 minutes of tab-switching now takes under 30 seconds.

DORA Metrics Dashboard calculates all four engineering performance metrics — Deployment Frequency, Lead Time for Changes, MTTR, and Change Failure Rate — using live Coral SQL queries. MTTR comes from PagerDuty, deployment frequency from GitHub, and change failure rate from a cross-source query joining GitHub deploys with Sentry fatal errors. Every metric has a sparkline chart showing the 8-week trend. The data is always live — no caching, no stale dashboards.

Pre-Merge Risk Scorer runs three Coral queries in parallel when you enter a PR number: it fetches the PR details from GitHub, counts recent Sentry errors in the same project, and checks PagerDuty for incidents in the same service over the last 30 days. It combines these into a 0–100 risk score with a breakdown of contributing factors and a recommendation. This is genuinely useful — it's the kind of signal that could have prevented countless Friday deploys gone wrong.

The "Query Glass" — making Coral visible

One thing I was intentional about: every time NEXUS executes a Coral query, the exact SQL appears in a side panel called the Query Glass. Users can see the query, copy it, and understand exactly what data was fetched. This does two things — it builds trust (no black box), and it showcases Coral's SQL interface as the actual product feature rather than hiding it in the backend.

Three custom source specs for the bounty

Beyond the bundled sources, I wrote three custom Coral source specs from scratch:

Buildkite (coral-sources/buildkite.yaml) — Coral doesn't bundle a CI/CD source, and this is a critical missing link. Buildkite appears in Coral's own homepage example query, so I built the spec to expose buildkite.builds, buildkite.pipelines, and buildkite.jobs. This completes the full incident story: PR merged → CI build broke → production error → PagerDuty incident.

Beehiiv (coral-sources/beehiiv.yaml) — For newsletter analytics. Exposes subscriber growth, post engagement stats (open rate, click rate, conversions), and UTM attribution data. The cross-source join with GitHub becomes interesting: did a product launch deploy correlate with a subscriber spike?

Dub (coral-sources/dub.yaml) — For link analytics. Exposes short link clicks, leads, sales revenue, and UTM parameters. When joined with Beehiiv on utm_campaign, you can see which campaign links actually converted to newsletter subscribers — a genuinely useful growth funnel query that no existing tool makes easy.

What Coral made possible that nothing else could

The honest answer is: without Coral, NEXUS is a chatbot that makes API calls one at a time and stuffs raw JSON into a context window. With Coral, it's an agent that reasons over structured, joined data from multiple live sources simultaneously — and the agent's context window stays focused on answers rather than raw API responses.

The 20% accuracy improvement and 2x cost efficiency numbers from Coral's own benchmarks aren't abstract to me — I felt it while building. The agent's answers with Coral are qualitatively better than what you'd get from individual API tool calls, because the data arrives already correlated, filtered, and structured.

The most exciting part isn't any single query I wrote. It's that NEXUS users can ask questions I never anticipated, and as long as the answer lives somewhere in the connected sources, Coral's SQL interface gives the agent the tools to find it.
How was your hackathon experience?:
Building NEXUS for the Pirates of the Coral-bean Hackathon was genuinely one of the most technically dense experiences I've had. The moment that stood out most was the first time a three-source Coral SQL JOIN — pulling from GitHub, Sentry, and PagerDuty simultaneously — returned correlated rows in under 2 seconds. I was skeptical that the abstraction would hold, and it did. That changed how I thought about the entire project.

The hardest part was the Gemini streaming + agentic loop. Getting tool-use calls to work mid-stream — execute a Coral query, get rows back, feed them to Gemini, continue streaming the answer — required careful state management on both the API and frontend side. The SSE protocol I built has five distinct event types just to handle that coordination cleanly.

The biggest design win was the Query Glass — showing the exact SQL the AI wrote in real time. I originally planned to hide it. Showing it turned out to be the most engaging part of every demo. It makes Coral the star, not a backend detail.

Writing the three custom source specs (Buildkite, Beehiiv, Dub) taught me the most about how Coral works at its core. The signals were all there, sitting in six different tabs that no human checks on every PR. Blast Radius checks all six in one query, scores the deploy risk 0–100, and posts the verdict on the PR before you merge.

The problem
Risk lives across GitHub, Sentry, Datadog, PagerDuty, Slack, and Linear. Correlating them by hand on every pull request is impossible, so teams ship blind and find out in the postmortem. Wiring six API clients into an agent is brittle, token-heavy, and nobody does it.

What it does
On every pull request (via a GitHub App webhook), Blast Radius:

Runs one Coral SQL query that joins six operational sources for the changed files and service.
Computes a deterministic risk score (0–100) from auditable, fixed weights — incidents, error budget, error volume, contested files — with no LLM deciding the number.
Uses Fireworks models to write a concise, engineer-to-engineer PR comment, then a second model verifies every claim against the source data so it can't hallucinate a metric.
Delivers everywhere it matters: a comment on the PR, a Slack alert, an auto-page to PagerDuty if the PR is critical, and a live dashboard — with a domain-expert reviewer recommended from real commit history.

Tech stack
Data plane: Coral (one SQL interface over GitHub, Sentry, Datadog, PagerDuty, Slack, Linear)
Inference: Fireworks AI (deepseek-v4-pro for narration, kimi-k2p5 for verification)
Agent: LangGraph (5-node pipeline) + deterministic Python scorer
Observability: Langfuse (full LLM tracing)
Backend: FastAPI (Python 3.12), Redis cache, GitHub App, Slack, PagerDuty Events API, n8n orchestration
Frontend: Next.js 15 + Tailwind v4 dashboard, Clerk auth
Deploy: Render blueprint

The GitHub App is installed and posts comments as blast-radius-ci[bot]; GitHub, Sentry, and PagerDuty are live through the real Coral CLI, producing genuine risk scores on real PRs (Datadog, Slack, and Linear use the identical connect-and-query pattern). Scores, findings, the expert recommendation, the Langfuse traces, the Slack alerts, and the PagerDuty page are all driven by real data, not mocks.

Six tools. One query. Zero surprises.
Describe how you have used Coral in your:
How Blast Radius uses Coral
Coral is the data plane of the entire product. Blast Radius answers one question on every pull request — "how likely is this to cause an outage?" — and that answer requires correlating signals that live in six different systems (GitHub, Sentry, Datadog, PagerDuty, Slack, Linear). Instead of writing and maintaining six API clients, each with its own auth, pagination, and rate-limit handling, we let Coral expose all of them as one SQL surface and ask for exactly the columns we need in a single query.

How it's wired
The FastAPI backend talks to the real Coral CLI (withcoral.com, installed via brew install withcoral/tap/coral). Our CoralClient shells out to:

coral sql "<SQL>" --format json
as an async subprocess and parses the JSON rows. Sources are connected once with coral source add (e.g. GITHUB_TOKEN=$(gh auth token) coral source add github), and their credentials stay in Coral's local state — nothing leaves the machine.

Inside the LangGraph agent, the CoralExecutor node runs the cross-source query for a PR and assembles the signal set the deterministic scorer consumes. We query Coral's real bundled-source schema (discovered via coral source info / information_schema), for example:

-- changed files + churn for the PR (github source)
SELECT filename, additions, deletions
FROM github.files
WHERE owner = $1 AND repo = $2 AND pull_number = $3;

-- domain expert by commit history (github)
SELECT author__login AS login, count(*) AS commits
FROM github.commits WHERE owner=$1 AND repo=$2 GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC;

-- live error volume (sentry)
SELECT COALESCE(SUM(count),0) AS total_events
FROM sentry.issues WHERE status = 'unresolved';

-- recent incident history (pagerduty)
SELECT title, urgency FROM pagerduty.incidents LIMIT 25;
Those results flow into a deterministic risk score, an expert recommendation, and the LLM-written PR comment. SENTINEL is an async, read-only security agent for open-source repositories. It monitors pull requests, dependency changes, GitHub Actions workflows, AI-agent config files, Slack/Jira approval context, and local security findings.

The problem we solve is that modern open-source attacks often do not look like normal code vulnerabilities. A harmless-looking PR can leak credentials in metadata, add a risky package, poison an AI-agent SKILL.md file, escalate workflow permissions, or introduce a typosquatted GitHub Action. SENTINEL catches these signals before they become incidents.

It ingests GitHub webhooks, writes canonical findings into DuckDB, mirrors queryable rows into JSONL for Coral, enriches events with Socket.dev, OSV.dev, npm/PyPI metadata, and mcp-scan, then scores threats deterministically and sends Discord/Slack alerts with clickable evidence links. It also provides a role-gated Discord /sentinel command for release-risk queries.
Describe how you have used Coral in your:
SENTINEL uses Coral as its cross-source correlation engine, the single layer that makes detection possible without any ETL, warehouse, or custom glue code.

The core of SENTINEL's threat detection is a SQL query that JOINs sentinel.audit_events (populated from GitHub webhooks) against slack.messages, jira.issues, and duckdb.supply_chain_findings simultaneously. The detection logic is expressed entirely as SQL. A NULL result on the Slack and Jira LEFT JOINs IS the finding. An OAuth grant with no corresponding approval thread shows up as slack_approval = NULL. No rules engine, no ML. Just relational logic across live sources.

identity_map.yaml is loaded as a Coral file source and JOINed against every query to resolve cross-system identities, mapping GitHub handles to Slack IDs, Jira handles, and Workspace emails. Without this JOIN, cross-source correlation would break on any real-world identity fragmentation.

External enrichment results from Socket.dev, mcp-scan, and the npm/PyPI registry are written to DuckDB tables and exported as JSONL via atomic rename. Coral reads these as file sources and JOINs them against live GitHub and Slack data in the master query. All correlation happens in SQL, none in Python.

SENTINEL exposes a /sentinel Discord bot command where maintainers ask questions in plain English. The LLM classifies intent to one of seven pre-defined Coral macro views: vw_release_blockers, vw_supply_chain_risks, vw_oauth_ungoverned, vw_workflow_mutations, vw_actor_anomalies, vw_credential_exposure, vw_onboarding_pending. Coral executes the mapped view via MCP and returns a structured result set. No arbitrary SQL generation. All queries are bounded and schema-safe.

Coral runs in MCP mode, allowing SENTINEL's LLM layer to invoke Coral queries as tool calls. The LLM receives only field-filtered Coral result rows, never raw source data. This keeps the LLM in the narration role and Coral in the detection role, with a clean boundary between them.

SENTINEL ships three app-local Coral source specs: socket.yaml for the Socket.dev supply chain API, google_workspace.yaml for the Google Workspace Admin SDK OAuth grant audit log, and discord.yaml for alert delivery. Each spec extends Coral's queryable surface to a data source not covered by bundled connectors. All three pass coral source validate.

SENTINEL emits OpenTelemetry metrics (sentinel.alert.fired, sentinel.query.duration, sentinel.score) and exports them to Grafana, which is a bundled Coral source. Project description:
The Problem: Fragmented Developer Telemetry
Modern engineering teams suffer from tool fatigue and data fragmentation. When an application fails after a deployment, a team must look in multiple places:
Checking GitHub for the merged pull requests.
Checking Sentry or cloud logs for error traces.
Checking Slack to see who is on-call or discussing the incident.
Checking local build systems to verify binary and package optimization.
Correlating this data usually requires writing custom ETL pipelines, maintaining complex glue-code, setting up webhook servers, or writing endless API scripts. It introduces latency, credentials management complexity, and security risks.
The Solution: DevRadar
DevRadar is a real-time, local-first engineering intelligence console. Instead of building integrations for every tool, DevRadar uses Coral as a unified database interface.
With DevRadar, every external API, internal task tracker, and local log file is modeled dynamically as a virtual SQL table. Teams can run complex, cross-source analytical queries—such as correlating failed local test builds with corresponding merged GitHub pull requests—instantly, locally, and without writing a single line of backend integration logic.
Describe how you have used Coral in your:
Our architecture is built from the ground up to utilize Coral’s unique capabilities. Below is a breakdown of how Coral powers DevRadar:
A. Cross-Source Correlated SQL JOINs
The defining feature of DevRadar is its ability to perform relational joins across totally separate data structures. We execute queries that join live GitHub repository data with local metrics seamlessly:
code
SQL
SELECT 
    b.build_id, 
    b.commit_sha, 
    b.build_time_sec, 
    pr.title AS pr_title, 
    pr.author__name AS pr_author 
FROM local_metrics.perf_benchmarks b 
JOIN github.pull_requests pr ON pr.merge_commit_sha = b.commit_sha 
WHERE b.test_success_rate < 0.95;
Instead of fetching pages of JSON from GitHub and manually matching hashes against local file arrays, Coral acts as the query execution engine, performing this join over live sources.
B. Custom Coral Source Connector (DSL Version 3)
To demonstrate Coral’s extensibility, we developed a custom file-based connector using the DSL v3 specification (local_metrics.yaml).
The Config: It targets local JSON-Lines (.jsonl) files containing system build performance metrics.
Dynamic Environments: It reads from path locations dynamically via environment variables ({{env.METRICS_DIR_PATH}}).
The Table: Coral dynamically transforms these unstructured text files into a clean relational table (local_metrics.perf_benchmarks), complete with schema-enforced data types (Utf8, Float64).
C. Live Schema Discovery and Inspection
Rather than hardcoding table metadata, DevRadar leverages Coral’s internal system catalog. We query:
coral.tables to discover active and mounted sources.
coral.columns to map schema structures dynamically inside the frontend console.
This guarantees that if a developer mounts a new source (e.g., Slack or Linear) into their Coral installation, DevRadar automatically detects the schemas and populates the sidebar without requiring any software updates.
D. Natural Language AI Agent to SQL Generation
Using Coral, we designed an intelligent assistant that acts as a natural language compiler.
The developer asks a question (e.g., "What pull requests broke our build times?").
The AI assistant maps the request to Coral schema tables.
It generates clean, standard ANSI SQL.
It calls our Express backend, which executes the command directly via the local coral CLI using shell child processes (coral sql --format json -- "<query>").
This architecture eliminates the need for expensive vector embeddings and allows LLMs to query live data directly and safely, with zero data ever leaving the user's local workspace.
E. Native Authentication & Caching Handling
We offloaded authentication, pagination, and rate-limiting completely to Coral. DevRadar doesn't handle GitHub personal access tokens or Sentry API keys; Coral manages them locally and handles smart caching. This minimizes credentials exposure and ensures our application remains light, secure, and resilient.

Project description:

Given that Coral is providing an optimised way via its amazing SQL like queries that helps the agentic system access different tools themselves and provide the right information to the user, we have provided here a combination of Coral + AI + N8N + Slack.

The project revolves around making the N8N pipelines autonomous via the agents, which is FIRST OF ITS KIND in the world. We are providing the following

2. Real time execution logs
3. On error real time alerts.
4. QnA for stopping, inspecting, executing workflows

And many more...

And the best part is Coral is acting like the main backbone of the whole project.
Describe how you have used Coral in your:
Coral is the analytical command center for this project. It is not being used as a generic side tool or as a branding layer. The n8nlysis project, uses Coral to create one consistent evidence surface over n8n workflows and executions so the AI, the frontend, and the alert pipeline all reason from the same source of truth.

The project deliberately splits responsibilities like this:

1. Coral: read-first analytical layer
2. Vertex Express: human-facing reasoning layer
3. n8n API: workflow runtime and mutation layer
4. Slack webhook: notification delivery layer
5. Frontend: operator visibility and manual control layer

That split matters because Coral is excellent at giving the project a queryable operational view, but the current n8n Coral source is not the mutation plane. Workflow edits, publish actions, archive actions, and execution lookups that need live runtime payloads still go through the n8n API.

When the portal needs evidence, it should ask Coral first.

When the portal needs to mutate or inspect full live runtime payloads, it should use the n8n API.

This is why the recommendation flow and alert flow both start from Coral evidence, then enrich with n8n JSON when necessary.


The project supports both local and remote n8n targets. The community Coral n8n source currently exposes the same schema name, n8n, which means both targets cannot safely share one Coral config root.

The fix in this MVP is target-scoped Coral config directories:

Local Coral profile: storage/coral/config
Remote Coral profile: storage/coral/remote-config
Each profile still exposes the same schema name, n8n, but the profile itself is target-specific.

Why this is the chosen design
It avoids source-name collisions.
It keeps Coral queries identical across targets.
It lets the frontend switch between local and remote without inventing a second SQL schema.
It keeps the recommendation and alert code simple, because both can ask for n8n.workflows and n8n.executions while only the profile changes underneath.

Project description:
Sales teams in India lose deals they should have won. Not because they didn't work hard. Because nobody connected the dots in time.
The client stopped replying 10 days ago. The key contact just switched jobs. The budget approver never joined a single call. A competitor got mentioned three times in the team chat this morning. Each of these alone is a yellow flag. Together they are a dead deal. And by the time anyone notices - the quarter is already gone.
We built Deal Cortex - a 6-agent AI system that watches every deal across every data source simultaneously and tells your sales team exactly where to focus, every single morning.
It works like this. A sales manager asks a plain English question - "Which deals are we actually going to close this month?" Six specialised AI agents get to work instantly. One understands the question. One decides which data sources matter. One writes a precise query across all of them. One scores every deal on 10 real signals. One tracks whether deals are getting better or worse week over week. One packages everything into a Slack message, a Word document, a PowerPoint deck, and updates your sales records - automatically.
Every deal gets a score. Green means healthy. Amber means watch it. Red means act today. Not based on what someone typed into the CRM. Based on what the emails, calls, meetings, team chat, and LinkedIn activity actually show.
Four signals that no other tool catches together:
A deal where you are only talking to one person at the client company - and that person just started looking for a new job - gets flagged immediately. A deal that was scoring 85 three weeks ago and is now at 55 is treated differently from a deal that has been average all along. A deal closing this quarter with no meeting scheduled in the next two weeks gets its own red flag. And every single CRM update is permanently logged with a full snapshot of every signal at that exact moment - so there is never a question of why a deal was marked safe when it wasn't.
This is not a dashboard. It is an intelligence system that gets smarter with every deal your team wins or loses.
Describe how you have used Coral in your:
Coral is not a supporting tool in our project. It is the foundation everything is built on.
The core problem we were solving is a data fragmentation problem. A sales deal lives across five completely separate systems - a CRM, an email client, a call recording tool, a team chat, and a professional network. Every existing sales intelligence tool picks one of these and builds around it. We needed all five at once.

Coral gave us that in a single SQL interface.

One query instead of five API calls. Our Query Agent - powered by CrewAI and Groq - dynamically writes a Coral SQL query at runtime based on what the sales manager actually asked. Not a hardcoded template. A fresh query every time, written by an LLM that knows the exact Coral schema. That query JOINs Salesforce deal records with Gmail reply timestamps with Gong sentiment scores with Slack competitor mentions with LinkedIn job change signals - in one shot. Without Coral this would be five separate API integrations, five rate limit budgets, five authentication flows, and five data normalisation problems.

The JOIN that matters most. Our most powerful signal - the one that catches deals about to die - requires three sources simultaneously. We correlate a contact's LinkedIn job change date with the Gmail thread silence duration and the Gong sentiment trend. No single tool has ever been able to do this join before. Coral makes it a three-line SQL query.

Schema as LLM context. We feed the Coral schema directly into our Query Agent's system prompt. This means the LLM writes precise, valid SQL against real table and column names instead of hallucinating field names. The schema becomes a contract between the agent and the data layer - and Coral enforces it.

From mock to live in one swap. During development we used five CSV files as mock Coral data. Every agent, every scorer, every output was built against the exact column names that Coral exposes. When we wrote the real Gmail source spec, the only change was the data source - zero changes to any agent logic. That is the power of Coral's unified interface. The SQL stays the same whether the data comes from a CSV file or a live Gmail OAuth connection.

Coral handles what agents should never handle. Pagination, authentication, rate limiting, response normalisation - all of this lives in the Coral source spec, not in our agent code. Our agents are clean. They ask questions in SQL. Coral handles everything underneath. This separation made our codebase dramatically simpler and our agents dramatically more reliable.

The result is a system where a single natural language question triggers one Coral query that reads five live data sources, returns clean joined data, and feeds six AI agents - in under 15 seconds.
How was your hackathon experience?:
It started with confusion honestly - staring at the Coral docs thinking "okay what do I actually build with this?"

Then the ideas started coming. Too many of them. Customer success dashboards, recruiting pipelines, financial risk monitors - everything felt possible once you realise you can JOIN any five data sources with one SQL query.

Picking one was the hardest part. We went back and forth. But we kept coming back to the same pain point - sales teams losing deals they should have won because nobody connected the dots in time. That felt real. That felt worth building.

Once we locked in the idea everything moved fast. The agent pipeline came together naturally. Coral handled the data layer so cleanly that we could focus entirely on the intelligence - the scoring, the momentum tracking, the audit trail. Things we actually cared about building.

There were rough moments. A merge conflict at 2am between two features touching the same scoring function. A path error that took way too long to debug. The usual.

But that first moment when a plain English question triggered six agents, pulled from five data sources, and landed a fully formatted Slack digest, Word doc, and PowerPoint all at once - that made every frustrating hour worth it.
Coral gave us the foundation. We built the story on top of it. Genuinely one of the most satisfying things we've shipped.

Project description:
Yelp Fusion → Coral: a new SQL source spec for local business intelligence.

I built and contributed a brand-new community source spec that turns the Yelp Fusion API into a first-class Coral SQL source. With one YAML manifest, any Coral-powered agent can now query Yelp businesses, reviews, events, categories and autocomplete suggestions as normal SQL tables and search functions — no ETL, no glue code, no warehouse, fully local.

The spec exposes 3 provider-ranked search functions (search_businesses, search_events, autocomplete_terms) using Coral DSL v3's `kind: search` shape, plus 4 detail tables (business_details, business_reviews, event_details, categories) with required-filter routing into path params. Deeply nested Yelp JSON is flattened using Coral's `__` convention (coordinates__latitude, location__city, user__profile_url, etc.) and array fields are projected via `join_array_path` so they read cleanly in SQL.

Auth is HeaderAuth Bearer with the Yelp API Key stored in the OS keychain. Pagination is `offset` with the provider-enforced 50-row page cap. Two `test_queries` against the free Yelp Fusion tier pass on first install (`coral source test yelp` → 2 declared · 2 passed · 0 failed).

The contribution targets the "Chart New Waters" bounty: a new source spec, submitted as a PR to withcoral/coral, validated end-to-end with `coral source lint` and `coral source test`, with a full README explaining setup, usage, cross-source JOIN examples (Yelp × Slack, Yelp × Google Calendar, Yelp × GitHub) and notes on Yelp's gated endpoints. PR: https://github.com/withcoral/coral/pull/1094

Describe how you have used Coral in your:
This project IS a contribution to Coral itself — a brand-new community source spec for the Yelp Fusion API, written entirely against Coral's DSL v3 spec.

Specifically, I used Coral as follows:

1. Source spec authoring (DSL v3, backend: http)
   • inputs.YELP_API_KEY with kind: secret + credential.methods (type: source_config) for safe local storage in the OS keychain
   • base_url + auth.type: HeaderAuth with Authorization: Bearer {{input.YELP_API_KEY}}
   • Three search functions declared with `kind: search` + `search_limits` (default_top_k, max_top_k, max_calls_per_query) and named-arg bindings so SQL callers use `yelp.search_businesses(location => '…', term => '…')` syntax
   • Four normal tables (business_details, business_reviews, event_details, categories) declared with `filters` blocks where `id` / `business_id` are required, and request.path templated with `{{filter.id}}` to route into Yelp's /businesses/{id} and /events/{id} endpoints
   • pagination.mode: offset with offset_param/limit query_param, respecting Yelp's max-50-per-page contract
   • Deeply nested Yelp JSON flattened with the `__` column-naming convention (coordinates__latitude, location__city, user__profile_url, …)
   • `join_array_path` over the `categories[]` array to expose `category_aliases` / `category_titles` as comma-joined Utf8
   • `from_filter` expression to echo `business_id` back into review rows so SQL JOINs stay clean
   • Two `test_queries` against free-tier Yelp endpoints, declared in the manifest so `coral source test yelp` runs them on demand

2. Coral CLI workflow
   • `coral source lint sources/community/yelp/manifest.yaml` → catches DSL errors locally with no credentials
   • `coral source add --file sources/community/yelp/manifest.yaml` → secrets land in the OS keychain (not on disk)
   • `coral source test yelp` → 2 declared · 2 passed · 0 failed (screenshot in the Discord submission post)
   • `coral sql "…"` → live SQL against Yelp returning real businesses, ratings, addresses, photos
   • `coral.tables` and `coral.table_functions` queried to verify the schema Coral sees matches the spec

3. Cross-source design intent
   The whole point of using Coral here is that a Yelp query becomes JOIN-able with every other Coral source. The README ships with cross-source example queries (Yelp × Slack threads, Yelp × Google Calendar lunch meetings, Yelp × GitHub commit cities) that turn into single-statement SQL once the source is installed — no agent context bloat, no glue code, no warehouse round-trip.

The submitted PR (https://github.com/withcoral/coral/pull/1094) lands the manifest + README under sources/community/yelp/. Both files were authored entirely against Coral's published source-spec reference and iterated against `coral source lint` until clean.
How was your hackathon experience?:
Incredible build experience. Coral's "any API as SQL" model is exactly the right abstraction for agentic data access — I built and shipped a complete Yelp Fusion source spec (3 search functions + 4 detail tables, full nested-JSON flattening, HeaderAuth, offset pagination, end-to-end test_queries) in a single hackathon session, mostly because Coral's DSL v3 lets you describe an API declaratively instead of writing yet another bespoke client.

The dev loop is genuinely fast: `coral source lint` catches schema mistakes locally before you ever spend a credential, `coral source add --file` validates inputs at install time, and `coral source test` gives you a clean PASS/FAIL on declared test_queries so the source has a real contract. The fact that the result is queryable as plain SQL, joinable with every other Coral source, and runs 100% locally is a different category of developer experience than gluing together MCP servers and API wrappers by hand.

Huge thanks to the WeMakeDevs and Coral teams for organising this. The "Pirates of the Coral-bean" framing was great branding, the documentation was clear, and the source-spec authoring path (custom-source guide + skill + bundled sources as reference) made it possible to ship something polished in a few hours. Project description:
Corsair: The Local-First Student Command Center
The Problem
Student developers face a constant battle with context-switching. Between tracking academic assignments in Notion, managing pull requests on GitHub, and balancing hackathon sprints, critical tasks easily slip through the cracks. Traditional productivity tools require manual syncing or brittle, expensive cloud integrations (ETL pipelines) to connect these disparate data sources, which is overkill for a student's workflow.

The Solution
Corsair is a local-first, unified command center designed specifically for student developers. It serves as a single pane of glass that aggregates, analyzes, and ranks active tasks across multiple platforms in real-time, completely eliminating the need to tab-switch between workspace apps.

Key Features

The Unified Priority Queue: Corsair calculates a dynamic "Urgency Score" by cross-referencing upcoming academic deadlines with active repository issues. It generates a single, ranked list that tells you exactly what to work on next.

Zero-ETL Architecture: Instead of building complex API pollers and cloud databases, we integrated the Coral Query Engine. Corsair uses Coral to treat local files (like a Notion .csv export) and live GitHub data as standard SQL tables.

Hackathon Focus Mode: With the flip of a switch, the dashboard deprioritizes standard academic tasks and isolates high-urgency sprint issues, keeping you locked into your developer workflow when the clock is ticking.

Command Deck UI: A lightweight, highly responsive frontend built with a cyberpunk-inspired glassmorphism aesthetic to provide a true "cockpit" experience.

Under the Hood (How We Built It)
The backend is powered by FastAPI, serving as the bridge between the UI and our local data. The core innovation is our Python subprocess integration with the Coral CLI. When the dashboard requests data, FastAPI commands Coral to execute a relational JOIN query directly against our raw local files. Coral processes this instantly on the local machine without requiring a heavy, hosted database.

The synthesized payload is then served to our custom HTML/CSS/JS frontend. To ensure maximum reliability during live demonstrations, the FastAPI layer includes a failsafe protocol that seamlessly serves structured fallback data if the local environment encounters execution timeouts, ensuring the dashboard remains 100% operational at all times.
Describe how you have used Coral in your: We integrated the Coral Query Engine as the core relational data layer of our application to achieve true cross-source data integration with zero ETL overhead.  Instead of writing complex API pollers, webhooks, or setting up a heavy hosted database to sync data between a user's workspace apps, we treated our raw, local data streams as instant SQL tables using Coral.  Here is exactly how it works under the hood:The Data Sources: We maintained local data dumps, including our Notion task logs (notion_tasks.csv).  The Query Execution: Inside our FastAPI backend (main.py), we configured a live execution channel that calls the Coral CLI via a Python subprocess. When a user loads or refreshes the dashboard, FastAPI commands Coral to run a native SQL query: SELECT name, due as due_date, sprint, priority FROM notion_tasks.  Zero-ETL Joining: Coral processes this query directly on the raw files instantly on the local machine. It joins the contextual metadata—matching academic assignment deadliness against active development tracking.  Dynamic UI Rendering: The parsed JSON output from Coral is piped straight to our glassmorphic index.html frontend. This allows the dashboard to dynamically calculate real-time urgency percentages, handle our "Hackathon Focus Mode" filters on the fly, and build a unified Priority Queue without a single cloud database dependency.  By offloading the entire data aggregation and parsing workload to Coral, we cut our backend integration footprint down to a single lightweight file, delivering a lightning-fast, local-first application

Meridian is an AI-powered productivity dashboard designed for software engineers and technical leads who need a single, unified view of their work across GitHub, Slack, Linear, Notion, and their calendar. The core philosophy is that AI should function as a layer of perception, not a conversational assistant. A persistent Pulse Bar delivers rotating AI-generated insights from live data. Describe how you have used Coral in your:
How We Used Coral in ContextOS
ContextOS uses Coral as its universal data layer — the single interface through which all external platform data is queried, normalized, and fed into the intelligence pipeline.
SQL as the common language across every tool
Instead of writing separate API integrations for each platform, we used Coral's SQL CLI to query Google Calendar, Gmail, Slack, Notion, Discord, and GitHub through a unified SQL interface. Every data source becomes a table. A morning briefing that previously would have required 6 different API clients, auth flows, and response parsers was reduced to straightforward SQL queries like:
sqlSELECT summary, start_date_time FROM google_calendar.events LIMIT 10
SELECT name, unread_count FROM slack_messages.unread WHERE unread_count > 0
SELECT number, title, state FROM github.pulls WHERE owner = 'GaneshBamalwa' AND repo = 'coralHackathon'
Custom Source Contribution
We wrote a full custom Discord source spec (manifest.yaml) that exposed Discord's REST API v10 as four queryable tables — guilds, channels, messages, and guild_members — complete with cursor pagination, required filter handling, and full column documentation. This source was submitted as an open source contribution to the Coral community catalog (PR #1060 on withcoral/coral).
We also wrote a custom slack_messages source that extended Coral's bundled Slack source with message history and unread count capability using the conversations.history API endpoint — something the bundled source didn't support.
Credential injection on Windows
Running Coral as a child process in a Node.js backend on Windows meant the OS keychain was unavailable for credential storage. We solved this by building a buildCoralEnv() function that injects all OAuth tokens directly as environment variables into the Coral binary's process context, bypassing the Windows keychain entirely using shell: false on every exec() call.
NLP to SQL via Meridian Lens
We built a natural language query engine called Meridian Lens that uses Gemini 2.5 Pro to translate plain English questions into valid Coral SQL, executes them live against all connected sources, and uses Groq to format the raw results into a clean readable response. The entire schema context — every table, every real column name verified directly from coral.columns — is fed to the LLM so it generates accurate queries every time.
Real-time intelligence synthesis
All Coral query results from every source are aggregated in a single backend pass, enriched with derived signals (back-to-back meetings, emails from today's attendees, overdue Notion tasks, recent Discord activity), and sent to Gemini 2.5 Pro to synthesize a cross-source Morning Briefing — not a summary of each tool in isolation, but genuine reasoning across everything happening at once.

Project description:
StudyAgent: The Context-Aware AI Study Coach
Tagline: Stop switching tabs. StudyAgent connects your Google Workspace and Notion into a single, intelligent AI chat interface powered by Coral and Gemini.

⚠️ The Problem
As students, our academic lives are fragmented. Lecture notes live in Google Drive, exam dates are buried in Google Calendar, syllabus updates are in Classroom, and personal study guides are scattered across Notion. The friction of finding information often takes more energy than actually studying it. Most AI assistants operate in a vacuum—you have to manually feed them context every time you want help.

💡 The Solution
StudyAgent is an intelligent, context-aware study coach that completely eliminates context-switching. By directly integrating with the tools you already use, the agent acts as a collaborative partner that already knows your schedule, your upcoming tests, and your syllabus.

✨ Key Features
Unified Workspace Sync: Instantly visualize and connect Google Calendar, Google Classroom, Google Drive, and Notion right from the sidebar.

Contextual Retrieval: Ask questions and get answers grounded in your actual course material. The agent pulls real-time data from your Notion pages and Google Docs.

Proactive Quick Actions: Generate study plans, summarize the latest lecture notes, or create rapid-fire review quizzes with a single click.

Dual-Model Intelligence: Built-in smart switching allows users to toggle between lightning-fast responses (gemini-2.5-flash) and deep, complex reasoning (gemini-2.5-pro).

🛠️ How We Built It (Tech Stack)
AI & Orchestration: Built for the WeMakeDevs Hackathon using Coral as the data-fetching bridge and Gemini 2.5 for natural language processing and reasoning.

Frontend: React, Tailwind CSS, and Shadcn UI. Designed with a sleek, dark-mode interface optimized for late-night study sessions.

Backend: Node.js/Express server handling secure OAuth callbacks, API routing, and agent orchestration.

🚧 Challenges We Conquered
Building a production-ready agent required solving real architectural hurdles:

Strict OAuth 2.0 Flows: Navigating complex redirect URI strictness to secure seamless connections between local development environments, Google Cloud Console, and Notion Developer portals.

API Rate Limiting (Error 429): Engineering around the constraints of free-tier API limits by implementing custom frontend UI throttling (cooldown states) and robust backend retry logic to ensure uninterrupted user experience.

🚀 What's Next
Cloud Deployment: Migrating local authentication to managed services (like Clerk) for true multi-tenant production access.

Vector Embedded Textbooks: Implementing local vector databases to chunk and index massive textbooks from Drive, bypassing Token-Per-Minute restrictions.

Collaborative Study Rooms: Enabling study groups to share a singular "Agent Canvas" to cross-reference notes and synchronize group project deadlines.
Describe how you have used Coral in your:
n your StudyAgent architecture, Coral acts as the crucial middle layer—the "data-fetching bridge"—between your React frontend, the Gemini reasoning engine, and the external data sources like Google Workspace and Notion.

Here is the step-by-step breakdown of exactly how Coral is operating inside your stack:

1. Defining the "Source Specs" (The Blueprints)
You use Coral by writing YAML configurations (Source Specs) that teach it how to talk to specific APIs. Instead of hardcoding fetch requests in Node.js, your YAML files tell Coral exactly which endpoints to hit (like the Google Classroom API) and how to filter that data, such as mapping course IDs to specific coursework.

2. Managing the OAuth Handshake
Instead of building complex API authentication from scratch for every single service, Coral helps handle the secure connections. It works alongside your backend routing to manage those strict OAuth 2.0 redirect URIs (/api/auth/callback), ensuring users can securely grant access to their Google Cloud and Notion Developer portals.

3. The Two-Stage Agent Pipeline
This is where Coral's integration really shines. When a user asks StudyAgent a question, you are using Coral to split the workload:

Stage 1 (Translation): Gemini takes the user's natural language question ("When is my next exam?") and translates it into actionable parameters or filters.

Stage 2 (Execution & Retrieval): Coral takes those parameters, executes the actual API call to Google Calendar or Notion, and fetches the raw data.

Stage 3 (Reasoning): Coral feeds that raw data back to Gemini (2.5-flash or 2.5-pro), which synthesizes it into the final, human-readable response that gets rendered in your chat UI.

Essentially, you are using Coral as the "hands" to securely reach out and grab the data, while Gemini acts as the "brain" to understand the user and explain the findings.

Project description:
Local SaaS Analytics Powered by Coral
SaaS teams are drowning in fragmented data. Revenue lives in Lemon Squeezy. Code activity lives in GitHub. Product health metrics live somewhere else. Every morning, someone manually stitches it all together just to answer one question: how are we actually doing?

Jackdaw is a local-first analytics platform that answers that question instantly. It gives SaaS teams a single operational dashboard — Ship Radar for real-time metrics, Morning Brief for AI-generated daily summaries, Issue Triage for impact-ranked GitHub issues, and Ask Anne for natural language queries across all your data sources at once.

The entire intelligence layer is built on Coral. Coral sits between Jackdaw and every data source — GitHub, Lemon Squeezy, your own database — and handles auth, pagination, schema mapping, and natural language to SQL translation. When a user asks "which paying customers have open GitHub issues this week?", Coral generates a JOIN across Lemon Squeezy and GitHub, executes it locally, and returns a clean result in seconds. No API glue. No ETL pipeline. No data ever leaves your machine.
Describe how you have used Coral in your:
Coral is the core data layer that makes Jackdaw possible. Rather than building bespoke API integrations for each data source, we use Coral as a unified SQL runtime that sits between Jackdaw and every external system.
We connect Coral to three sources — GitHub, Stripe, and a local metrics database — and expose all of them as queryable SQL schemas. Jackdaw's backend never calls a raw API directly. Every data fetch goes through Coral SQL, which means Coral handles authentication, pagination, rate limiting, and schema mapping automatically.
The Ask Anne feature is built entirely on Coral's MCP server. When a user types a natural language question, the request goes to an agent that uses Coral over MCP to discover available schemas and tables, generate the appropriate SQL, and execute it locally. Cross-source queries — like joining paying customers from stripe.customers with open issues from github.issues on email address — work out of the box because Coral presents every source as a single unified schema layer. There is no ETL, no intermediate storage, and no data ever leaves the machine.
Ship Radar, Morning Brief, and Issue Triage are each powered by scheduled Coral SQL queries that run on a local timer and feed the dashboard. Coral's query pushdown and caching keep these fast without hammering upstream APIs.
Stripe and GitHub are both bundled Coral sources, which meant zero integration work on our end — we ran coral source add stripe and coral source add github, configured our keys, and both sources were immediately queryable as SQL schemas. That's the compounding value of Coral's bundled source library: the hard part is already done.

Know before you ship. Powered by Coral + an LLM of your choice (Groq Llama 3.3 70B by default; Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6 supported).

What errors will block this release? (Sentry)
Are all planned features actually merged? (Linear ⋈ GitHub)
What did the last few merges break in production? (GitHub ⋈ Sentry)
What is the team actually saying about the release? (Slack)
Are we on track this sprint? (Linear)
Then it asks an LLM (Groq's Llama 3.3 70B by default, or Anthropic's Claude Sonnet 4.6 if you'd rather) to look at all of that and give you one recommendation: SHIP / SHIP WITH CAUTION / HOLD plus a 0–100 score.

Project description:
Meridian is a personal intelligence dashboard built for people who work across too many tools at once. GitHub, Slack, Notion, Calendar, Gmail, Discord, as well as our custom sources pushed to the repository - chromium and firefox sources, each one holds a piece of your day, but none of them talk to each other. Meridian connects all of them into a single, beautifully designed command center that tells you what is happening, what is overdue, and where your attention should go next.

The foundation is the Coral SQL Engine, which lets Meridian query your tools directly using standard SQL against live data. There is no intermediate database, no stale cache, no brittle per-service integration to maintain. Every insight Meridian surfaces is pulled fresh from the source at the moment you need it. On top of that data layer, Vertex AI (Gemini 2.5 Pro) generates a personalized Morning Briefing every day, synthesizing your calendar events, unread emails, and open tasks into a clear, prioritized summary of what the day actually looks like.

Beyond the briefing, Meridian helps you see patterns in your work that are easy to miss when you are heads down. Focus Debt tracking visualizes how your planned work compares to what got completed over the past seven days, so attention sinkholes become visible before they become problems. The Unfinished Loops view flags items that have been sitting open too long and gathering activity without resolution. And when you want to go deeper, the Meridian Lens lets you ask questions in plain English and instantly translates them into live Coral SQL queries, powered by Groq. The whole experience is designed to reduce the mental overhead of staying on top of your work, so you can spend less time figuring out what to do and more time actually doing it.
Describe how you have used Coral in your:
Meridian uses Coral as its universal data layer, the single interface through which all external platform data is queried, normalized, and fed into the intelligence pipeline.
SQL as the common language across every tool.
Instead of writing separate API integrations for each platform, we used Coral's SQL CLI to query Google Calendar, Gmail, Slack, Notion, Discord, and GitHub through a unified SQL interface. Every data source becomes a table. A morning briefing that previously would have required 6 different API clients, auth flows, and response parsers was reduced to straightforward SQL queries like:
sql SELECT summary, start_date_time FROM google_calendar.events LIMIT 10
SELECT name, unread_count FROM slack_messages.unread WHERE unread_count > 0
SELECT number, title, state FROM github.pulls WHERE owner = 'GaneshBamalwa' AND repo = 'coralHackathon'

Custom Source Contribution

We wrote a full custom Discord source spec (manifest.yaml) that exposed Discord's REST API v10 as four queryable tables, guilds, channels, messages, and guild_members,  complete with cursor pagination, required filter handling, and full column documentation. This source was submitted as an open source contribution to the Coral community catalog (PR #1060 on withcoral/coral).

We also wrote a custom slack_messages source that extended Coral's bundled Slack source with message history and unread count capability using the conversations.history API endpoint, something the bundled source didn't support.
Credential injection on Windows
Running Coral as a child process in a Node.js backend on Windows meant the OS keychain was unavailable for credential storage. We solved this by building a buildCoralEnv() function that injects all OAuth tokens directly as environment variables into the Coral binary's process context, bypassing the Windows keychain entirely using shell: false on every exec() call.

NLP to SQL via Meridian Lens

We built a natural language query engine called Meridian Lens that uses Gemini 2.5 Pro to translate plain English questions into valid Coral SQL, executes them live against all connected sources, and uses Groq to format the raw results into a clean readable response. The entire schema context, every table, every real column name verified directly from coral.columns,  is fed to the LLM so it generates accurate queries every time.
Real-time intelligence synthesis

All Coral query results from every source are aggregated in a single backend pass, enriched with derived signals (back-to-back meetings, emails from today's attendees, overdue Notion tasks, recent Discord activity), and sent to Gemini 2.5 Pro to synthesize a cross-source Morning Briefing,  not a summary of each tool in isolation, but genuine reasoning across everything happening at once.

Project description:
SlopGuard catches hallucinated dependencies before they reach pip install.
AI coding assistants make up package names all the time. fastapi_magic_helper, coral-agent-utils, things that sound totally real. When one of those lands in a PR, two things can happen: your build breaks, or an attacker already registered that exact name (slopsquatting) and now you're installing malware.
SlopGuard scans your PR diff, pulls out every new import, and checks it against PyPI or npm. You get a clear HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW verdict per package, and it exits non-zero on anything HIGH so it works as a CI gate out of the box.
Built for the WeMakeDevs x Coral hackathon.
Describe how you have used Coral in your:
SlopGuard uses Coral as the data access layer for GitHub pull request analysis.

When a user runs a scan against a pull request, SlopGuard queries GitHub data through Coral using SQL instead of interacting directly with GitHub's REST APIs. Coral provides pull request metadata, changed files, and diff patches through a unified SQL interface, allowing SlopGuard to extract newly introduced imports and dependencies from a PR with a single query.

This eliminates the need to handle GitHub API authentication, pagination, rate limiting, and custom data-fetching logic. Once the dependency changes are identified, SlopGuard enriches them with package registry metadata from PyPI and npm, including package age, download activity, and existence checks, then computes a risk score to detect potential slopsquatting attacks.

In addition, we developed and submitted a custom PyPI Coral source specification, enabling package registry information to be queried through the same SQL-based workflow. This allows security analysis to combine GitHub pull request data and package registry metadata within a unified data model.

Coral was essential because it transformed GitHub and package registry data into queryable tables, letting us focus on security detection logic rather than API integration and infrastructure.

🛠️ The Coral Engine: Cross-Source Joins
The entire dashboard runs on a single, highly performant Coral SQL query joining six file-backed schemas. This demonstrates Coral's ability to seamlessly bridge heterogeneous data sources without setting up heavy ETL pipelines:

pagerduty_demo.incidents: Outage incident metadata, severity, and service owners.
github_demo.deploys: Deployment logs, SHAs, commit messages, and repository diff links.
datadog_demo.metrics: Telemetry and latency parameters (p95 latency, baseline bounds, error rates).
sentry_demo.issues: Automated application exception traces, stack traces, and issue links.
slack_demo.messages: Real-time team war-room communication history.
crawler_demo.evidence: External client-side screenshots, browser failures, and automated UX analysis scores.
The local fixtures are stored in data/ and loaded via Coral DSL v3 source specs in coral/sources/, keeping the demo 100% deterministic, offline-friendly, and credential-free!

The Replay SQL Query (sql/replay.sql)
SELECT 
    i.incident_id,
    i.title,
    i.severity,
    i.service,
    i.created_at,
    i.resolved_at,
    d.deploy_sha,
    d.deploy_message,
    d.diff_url,
    m.p95_latency_ms,
    m.baseline_p95_ms,
    m.error_rate,
    s.sentry_issue_id,
    s.error_message,
    s.event_count,
    s.issue_url,
    sl.war_room_author,
    sl.war_room_message,
    sl.war_room_url,
    c.before_screenshot,
    c.after_screenshot,
    c.diff_score
FROM pagerduty_demo.incidents i
LEFT JOIN github_demo.deploys d ON i.service = d.service AND d.created_at BETWEEN i.created_at - INTERVAL '10' MINUTE AND i.created_at
LEFT JOIN datadog_demo.metrics m ON i.service = m.service AND m.timestamp BETWEEN i.created_at - INTERVAL '5' MINUTE AND i.created_at + INTERVAL '10' MINUTE
LEFT JOIN sentry_demo.issues s ON i.service = s.service AND s.created_at BETWEEN i.created_at AND i.created_at + INTERVAL '10' MINUTE
LEFT JOIN slack_demo.messages sl ON sl.channel = 'sre-war-room' AND sl.timestamp BETWEEN i.created_at AND i.created_at + INTERVAL '15' MINUTE
LEFT JOIN crawler_demo.evidence c ON i.incident_id = c.incident_id;

Project description:
The Dependency Vulnerability Tracker is an AI-powered security agent that continuously monitors all software dependencies across a GitHub organization, cross-references them against the OSV vulnerability database, and enriches each finding with full organizational context — Slack discussions, GitHub issues, and Linear tickets — to answer not just "are you vulnerable?" but "does your team already know, is there a ticket, and what is the blast radius?"
Every 24 hours (or on manual trigger), the agent executes a single cross-source SQL query via Coral that JOINs package manifests, CVE records, Slack messages, GitHub issues, and Linear tickets; classifies each vulnerability into one of four triage buckets; auto-drafts Linear tickets for critical untracked findings; and posts a severity-bucketed digest to Slack
Describe how you have used Coral in your:
Coral is the data access layer for our security scan pipeline. Instead of calling GitHub, OSV, Slack, GitHub Issues, and Linear with separate HTTP clients and ad hoc pagination, we run SQL against Coral sources and treat the results like a small analytics database.

1. Custom Coral source for GitHub dependencies

We authored a custom HTTP source spec (coral/sources/deps.packages.yaml) that exposes GitHub Dependency Graph data as SQL tables:

deps.repos / deps.user_repos — discover repositories for an org or user
deps.repo_packages — SBOM package rows for a given owner + repo
This replaces hand-rolled GitHub API calls for repo discovery and SBOM fetching.

2. OSV via Coral

We register Coral’s OSV community source and query:

osv.query_by_version — match vulnerabilities to package + ecosystem + version during the primary scan
osv.vulns — fetch full advisory JSON by ID during enrichment (OsvClient)
3. CoralQueryEngine wrapper

Node spawns the Coral CLI (coral sql --format json) with:

Redis caching (SHA-256 cache keys, configurable TTL)
Timeouts and typed errors (CoralTimeoutError, CoralQueryError, CoralParseError)
Optional Zod validation on result rows
Logging of every query to SQLite (coral_query_logs)
Prometheus metrics (coral_query_duration_seconds, cache hits, errors)
4. Scan pipeline integration

On each scan, ScanOrchestrator:

Primary scan — Coral SQL against deps.repo_packages and osv.query_by_version (parallelized per package) to build PrimaryScanRow[] (repo, package, version, CVE, severity).
Enrichment — OsvClient uses Coral for detailed OSV records; AI fills summaries when needed.
Context aggregation — ContextAggregator runs registered SQL for Slack messages, GitHub issues, Linear tickets, and blast-radius (deps.repo_packages + monitored deps) to attach org context before triage.
Queries live in src/coral/queries/*.sql and are loaded via a QUERIES registry.

5. Runtime configuration

Before scans, CoralConfigWriter writes ~/.coral/config.yaml with GitHub/Slack/Linear credentials from our settings UI, sources_dir pointing at coral/sources, and Redis-backed Coral cache settings.

6. Resilience

Coral failures are handled per stage: repo/package/OSV lookups are skipped with warnings; context queries fall back to empty context; enrichment falls back to scan-row data if OSV lookup fails. The scan continues rather than failing entirely on a single Coral error.

Summary: Coral lets DVT express “scan all repos → list packages → match OSV → pull Slack/GitHub/Linear context” as SQL over federated sources, with one CLI, caching, and observability—while we keep business logic (triage, tickets, digests) in TypeScript.
